"IF YOU WOULD HAVE GOOD ADVICE
THE VERDICT OF THE HEART.
BY CHARLES GARVICE,
Author of "Her Heart's Desire," "In Cupid's Chains," "Just a Girl," "Nance," "The Out- cast of the Family," "A Coronet of Shame," dr%

so--!" He shrugged his shoulders, and smiled with a scornful pity. • Ralpls stood erect, every vestige of colour gone from his face, his eyes fixed on the Earl's, and , unconscious of Veronica's, which were upturned la him as if she were trying to read his thoughts, to learn the effect of the Earl's appeal. "If the man be rich it is bad enough for her; but you are poor—you condemn her to poverty. Can you endure to see her pine and fade under the terrible ordeal which poverty ordains for • every woman—to • see her, perhaps, wanting for food? Oh, it is possible, believe me ! " "My lord ! " broke from Veronica's lips; but Ralph did not speak. "You condemn her to a life of misery—" "No, no ! " breathed Veronica, but he dis- regarded the faint cry. • "Poverty means misery for such as she is. She has taated ease, luxury, admiration—the admiration of her own class. As the years— months—pass, do you think you will not realise all that this maess has cost her? Wait! You are above your class, Ralph Farringcion, an exceptional specimen ; but think of the others in your class, the men—and the women—with whom you will compel her to associate! She is proud —her pride is :only sleeping under the narcotic of her love for you. It will wake—oh, very soon, believe me !—and you will have to stand by and share the burden of her regret, of her shame! Come, man! If there is a spark of the nobility in you with which she credits you you , will not let her sacrifice, degrade herself— ! Veronica uttered a cry, but Ralph's hand grasped hers and forced, commanded her to silence. His face was white, his lips were set tightly. For a moment it seemed as if he were incapable of speech, but he held up his hand and said, sternly: "No more; I cannot bear it! You have said enough, my lord. As man to man you have snoken to me, as man to man I will answer you. You have torn the veil from my eyes. It is true, true, every word of it! Sacrifice— such a sacrifice —for me! No, no! You are right. I cannot do it."

Veronica rose, her eyes fixed on his. "Ralph!" she breathed imploringly. He took her hand and looked at her with all his anguish in his eyes. "He is right," he said hoarsely. do it." "You—you give me up ? " Her voice was scarcely audible, but it went through his heart. "Yes—no, no! "ho said, brokenly. "I cannot! It is too much to ask. As long as I live I must love you--you know it! But I will not drag you down, I will not—degrade you! I will go. I will try to make my way, to be less unworthy of _ _
"I cannot
. His voice broke and failed him for a moment, then, crushing down his emotion, he said, as a man speaks when he is setting out on a forlorn

hope: • "But you must remain free. There shall be no promise, no tie. I—l—release you!" She clung to his arm with both her hands and looked at him fixedly, all her soul in her gaze. "You—you surrender me ? " she said. "Then —then you do not love me!" The Earl had leant forward on his stick, watching the scene intently, following each phase of their emotion with the cold scrutiny of an analyst watching the process of some intricate experiment. "Veronica!" he said, almost reproachfully. "Come, come! Be fair. Don't drive him too hard." • She did not move her eyes from Ralph's face— ignored the Earl completely. "Answer me," she said, in a quivering voice. ; "It is because I love you!" responded Ralph. The Earl rose and touched Veronica's arm. "Go up to the house, Veronica," he said, quietly. She still clung to Ralph. "I will go—if you tell me," she said, in a strangely still voice. 'Ralph's face worked, and the power of speech seemed to fail him; then he loosened her hands • of their clasp and said, fiercely: "Yes—go ! " She looked at him for the space of a moment, then turned slowly and went towards the entrance. There she stopped and looked over her shoulder at him—a look which racked his heart and almost broke him down. But he loved her, loved her, and there was no response to that, her last appeal. With a deep sigh her hand went up to her throat as if she were choking, then she passed out. Ralph took a step after her, but the Earl moved slightly; and as if the movement had recalled Ralph to his sense of duty he stopped, and sinking on to the seat covered his face with his hands. The Earl stood before him, looking down at him with a strange regard. At last he said very gravely: "You have behaved very well—like a man, and an honest one. The ordeal has been a trying one; I will see that you are spared a repetition. Of course you will leave the place at once. I think your decision to go back to Australia a very good and sensible one. Need I say that I will make it easy for you to 41) so? In fact, it will afford me much pleasure to assist you to a future. My steward shall have instructions to forward you the sum of—let us say, £2OO a year while you remain out of England--" ' Ralph rose, his face haggard, his lips tightly drawn; Imit they opened with a bitter laugh. "It is the only mistake you have made, my iora," he said, quietly. "In one breath you tell me I have behaved as a man, an honest man, in the next you ask me to act as a cur ! Where I go is no business of yours. I refuse your bribe--" The Earl's face darkened. "I see. You will hang about the pla6e—" ; Ralph's face turned from white to red, then white again. "Not for a day, an hour longer than I can help ! " he broke in passionately. "Your lordship need have no fear of me. I have given my word and—l will keep it " The Earl looked at him steadily. "I believe • you," he said. He paused. "I was wrong in offering you money, and—l ask your pardon." He raised his hat as he spoke, then slowly left the arbour.

country that we could not follow the American plan with advantage. The Anti-Corset Crusade.—Dress reform is rather played out as a silly season" topic, and but little enthusiasm is aroused by the revival of the anti-corset campaign. There are, and always will be, women who go to extremes,but nine-tenths of all that is written and said against the corset, as it concerns the average woman, is nonsense. It might almost be thought that one could not have a neat waist and yet enjoy good health hut reasonably worn,the corset is not unhealthy. Modern dress requires the aid it affords, and a well- made and moderately loose corset greatly improves the walk and carriage, as well as ones appearance. Hats Tilted Forward.—The backward tilt has had a very brief vogue in Paris, and fashionable Parisiennes are now wearing their hats either quite straight and flat upon their heads, or slightly tilted over the face the latter nation being always in high favour among Frenchwomen. And without doubt, the slight shade thrown over the face by the forward tilt of our head- gear is invariably becoming. " Hate " arrangements are all very well for, the quite fresh, and pretty girl, but they should certainly not be lightly adopted by the average girl and woman. Extremes Again.—ln the matter of veils we are rush- ing off to the opposite extreme, for whereas the deep full veil has long been modish, the smart woman now only permits this accessory to reach midway between her mouth and chin. It is gathered up behind too, in a neat manner, the ends being lost among the trimmings on the hat. Provided the loose flowing veil is not greatly exaggerated there is no doubt about it being the more becoming arrangement, but leaders of fashion are tired of the flowing veil, and want a change—at any cost,

A Revival.--Cut steel is coming into vogue again, a nd is being utilised for hair ornaments, belts, buckles, handbags, etc. There is only one drawback to this pretty fashion, and that is the difficulty we experience in keep- ing steel free from damp and the consequent rust. MADGE.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
A CHARMING SHOOTING COSTUME

For a woman who shoots—and there are twenty who do at partridges and pheasants for one who does at grouse and deer. says the Sketch —a charming costume is in thick deep-red drill.. The skirt is quite tight and stitched with strap pings over each seam to below the hips, where it is cleverly arranged in a series of close pleats that shew only as the wearer walks. The coat is Norfolk shape with a pleat down each side of the front and one at the back. Through these at the waist is passed a wide belt of deep red-brown patent leather. In front the right shoulder has a stock-rest piece of red-brown soft leather let in. The fronts of the coat are slightly open, shewing a white blouse of thin canvas embroidered in red and brown in Russia stitch. The hat is of burnt straw, almost Tyrolean in shape, with a band of soft brown silk and a double curled coque-feather in red and brown at the left side.

div.head: DRESS OF NINON-DE-SOIE.
div.p: DRESS OF NINON-DE-SOIE.

This charming gown is realised in golden- brown ninon-de-soie. The low-cut bodice is trimmed with bands of deep cream lace, dyed to match the material, and ornamented with a little gold thread and sequins, the two rows of lace being connected by a lattice of thin gold cord,

the lace over the shoulders being taken round beneath the arms. At the neck the bodice is filled in with fichu-like draperies of deep cream net. The full puffed sleeves are also of net, and finish at the elbow with narrow frills of lace and net. The skirt is pleated at the waist, and trimmed round the hem with a band of lace. THE EVERLASTING CLOTHES PROBLEM.

, It is a curious fact, declares a Globe fashion writer, that one may be quite pleased with one's clothes, and far from contemplating having any new ones, in the belief that one has plenty, and as soon as an invitation appears, which necessi- tates wearing them in another person's house, they suddenly all develop drawbacks and dis- abilities. There seem to be myriads of things of which one never thinks at home, and which may all be necessary away. In going to a new household, that is, where one has not visited be- fore. there are real complications to be consi- dered. Do they entertain much? Do they wear full evening dress for dinner? Do they go out often, and, if so, to what functions? Will there be tennis, or golf, or sea-bathing, or any other pursuits that require special costume?. Is it worse to appear followed by large boxes that must convince the frightened hostess that one has come to stay indefinitely; or to have too few clothes, and be dressed unsuitably? These are questions which the male mind describes as "women's nonsense about .plothes." How one longs now and then for a definite code of dress such as is enjoyed by the lordly male, and gives him his splendid superiority! Perhaps one day a benevolent hostess will have notepaper specially printed on which to write her invitations; in one corner the usual information as to station, telegraphic address, and telephone; in the other: "Motoring, tennis, bathing. Dinner, demi- toilet. No large parties. No general break- fast," or similar information.

div.head: HATLESS WOMEN IS CHURCH.
div.p: HATLESS WOMEN IS CHURCH.

The Rev. R. M. Marsh, vicar of Sheldon, in his parish magazine, calls attention to "the pain- ful duty imposed upon him at a recent wed- ding," when he had to request several ladies who had entered with uncovered heads to leave the church. The vicar has placed a notice at the church door requesting ladies not to enter with their heads uncovered. AUTUMN SHIRT BLOUSE.

In our sketch is shown a simple shirt blouse to wear with an autumn tweed costume. It in of fine white cashmere or nun's-veiling. and trimmed with bands of the material embroidered with thick silk to harmonise with the colour of the skirt; for instance, the mauve and purple colourings in a heather mixture tweed could be

repeated in the embroidery, in the cravat of soft satin, and the kid belt. The blouse has two em- broidered straps down the centre of the front, and the pointed yoke is also outlined with the embroidery. The fulness of the "skirts" is ar- ranged in the box-pleats at each side and at the centre of back, some small buttons, covered with mauve satin, being stitched to the top of each pleat. The full sleeves are drawn into loner. tight- fitting cuffs, trimmed with bands of embroidery.

div.head: WAY TO EARN A LIVING.
div.p: A WAY TO EARN A LIVING.

Superintending the decorations for the dinner- table seems to be a task within the reach of any artistic girl, says Mary Leigh in the World and His Wife; and although it may seem far too easy for anyone to earn a living at such work, it is nevertheless quite pos.sible to do so, and, when a, connection is worked up, a very comfortable income. Many ladies who entertain largely are far too much occupied with their social duties to have time to cast an eye on the laying of the dinner-table. They are glad to pay large sums to the really competent woman, with keen artistic tastes, who will arrange the floral decorations for the table, and superintend the laying of the meal. The work is far from arduous, and is most interesting and gratifying to anyone taking a pride in their own achievements.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

MUSHROOM ENTREE.-Trim and prepare two dozen fair-sized mushrooms for cooking. Re- move the stalks, chop them in small pieces, and fry in butter with an onion and a shallot, each being finely minced. When a good colour, stir in a dessertspoonful of chopped parsley, salt and pepper, a dessertspoonful of grated Parmesan cheese, and thicken with the yolks of two eggs. Place a little of the farce on each mushroom and smooth with a knife till level. Stand the mushrooms in a greased tin. sprinkle with baked oreaacrumns, lay smau pieces at ouLter- on me top, and cook in a moderate oven for twenty-five minutes. Serve in a circle with a thick brown Boum round.

div.head: CHAPTER XVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVII.
There was something appalling in the .old man's stone-like face, in the rigid, colourless lips, the face in which the only living thing seemed the eyes that gleamed like mica under the bent brows.

Veronica shrank back for a moment and caught her breath; but Ralph, after an instant of stupefaction, drew himself up and met the terrible eyes steadily. The 'Earl's glance passed over him and rested like a blight on Veronica. "I beg you to pardon me for this intrusion," he said, in a voice that struck like ice and cut like a whip in its infinite scorn. "I do not usually play the eavesdropper; but I may perhaps be excused on this occasion, seeing that the lady who has disgraced herself bears my name and is —or was—under my. care and in my charge." Ralph's face grew dark and his eyes flashed. "Disgraced, my lord!" broke from him. "Silence! " interrupted the Earl, as ieily impassive as before. "I wish to speak to—this lady. Leave us."

Ralph shook his head. "No," he said. "My place is by her side, my lord—until she tells me to go." Lord Lynborough bent his geze on Veronica. "Do you accept that ? " he asked, sternly, but with a kind of contemptuous indifference.
Veronica held out her hand to Ralph, and he took it.
"I do, my lord,' she said, in a low but perfectly clear voice. "The fault is mine. I accept all the responsibility." For the first time the Earl smiled—a bitter smile.

"I agree; • he said, "it is always the woman's fault, and she bears the consequences. That you encouraged this man I have no doubt. I had intended to address you alone, but as you choose that he should remain---" He shrugged his shoulders, paused a moment, then went on: "I gather from the words I heard to-day and yester- day—yes, I was here that you have con- descended to plight your troth to—my game- keeper ? " Veronica raised her head and regarded him cteadily,

"Yea!" she said, quietly, but as proudly as if Ralph had been her equal, her superior. The Earl inclined his head. "Thanks! You are candid. I imagine, from my eavesdropping, that this—intrigue has been in progress for soma time."

"If you mean that I have met him, have grown to love him—yes," replied Veronica. Each moment her courage was rising, the Denby spirit was in her low, clear voice, in her star-like eyes, and Ralph's heart was throbbing with pride in her. "You do not know all; you do not know that he saved my life—" "No, no ! " Ralph murmured, but she went on steadily, though her lips trembled. "That of all the men I have met, he is the bravest, the most kingly—" "I will ask you to spare me your rhapsodies," broke" in the Earl, with a wave of his hand. "We will accept your infatuation as an estab- lished fact. I merely asked from curiosity, and, yes; a desire to ascertain if it were possible for me to stretch out a hand and save you from the degradation to which you are sinking." Veronica's eyes flashed, and the colour dyed her cheek.
"Degradation, my lord!" "Do you wish to argue the point?" he said, deliberately. "You had best be seated, for it will take some few minutes."
She sank on to the seat, but motioned to Ralph to stand near her. As he did so he turned to the Earl.

"The fault is mine—l am answerable," he began hoarsely; but the Earl would not hear him. "Be silent! "he said, sternly. "I will address myself to you presently. Now, Veronica, we will take your infatuation for granted. I will do this man the justice to admit that the blame rests with you. I have heard every word. I know that he has struggled to resist you—that he failed is a tribute to your charms." She made to rise, stung by the cold, impassive voice, but sank down again with a gesture of forced patience.

"Thal you have exerted those charms to fascinate him I can well believe; no man forgets his place so soon unless he has had great encouragement, provocation. The devil made the woman to tempt, the man to yield.'" Ralph's face flamed, and he opened his lips, but the Earl motioned him to silence.

"You have tempted this man to the utmost— that he has yielded is no marvel. But have you considered the consequences? I think not. Women rarely do. Have you considered that, if you carry this thing to its mad conclusion, you leave the Court and my protection; you lose Wayneford and all I have willed to you; that you relinquish your place in society; that you become an outcast and a pariah?" Ralph uttered an exclamation, but Veronica took his hand and pressed it, and a heavenly smile. shone in her eyes.

"They are terribl; words, my lord," she said, "but they do not frighten me. I shall not become an outcast by marrying an honest man." Her voice trembled with suppressed passion, then grew steady. "My lord, I am not ungrateful—' _ . .
Re made a gesture of contemptuous repudia- tion.

"I do not forget all your kindness to me. I do not forget that you lifted me from a life of poverty to one of ease and luxury. You have been very good to me, and "—the tears rose to her eyes—"it hurts me that I should seem indifferent, ungrateful. But, oh, my lord, I—l cannot help it! I—l love him with all my heart and soul. Let the consequences be what they may, I cannot give him up. All the luxury in the world would be of no use to me without him. The consequences? Yes, I accept them. lam ready to share his life, to return to the old poverty, the old hard life—Ah, but it will be no longer hard if he will share it with me! " Ralph's heart throbbed, and he marvelled how any man could look upon that lovely face, listen to that sweet voice, unmoved.

The Earl was still like' a stone as he bent his head with icy courtesy. "And I thought you proud ! " he said, as if with self-contempt. "Proud!" she echoed, as if she were looking back on her past Ve—a self that had slipped from her for ever. "Yes, I suppose I was." A smile shone in her eyes. "Love casts out pride, my lord," she added, softly. The Earl shrugged his shoulders. "A noble sentiment," he said. "I have no more to say to you. Now, sir, for the few words I shall con- descend to address to you." Ralph drew his eyes slowly from the face of the woman he loved and fixed them on the Earl's, ' and the two men regarded each other as duellists look into each other's faces when the sword play begins; then the Earl's eyes grew contemplative and his frown deepened. "There must be something in you out of the common to have won this lady's heart," he said; "and I will try and forget that you are my servant, and -appeal to you— yes, appeal to you— as if we were for the moment on equal terms. At any rate, I will speak as man to man." Ralph flushed, and waited. The Earl was silent while one could count twenty, then he said, slowly, calmly: "My niece scorns the consequences of this mad act. But you? I take it that you—love her. It was a hard word to utter, and it fell with a metallic note from his bloodless lips. "Have you, too, considered what this infatua- pon of hers will cost her—not you, but her Oh, be silent, until I have finished. Can you, who love her, bear to see her degraded from the position in which she was born; can you accept the sacrifice she is prepared to make? Are you prepared to take advantage of her weakness for you? Think! The sacrifice will not be momentary, temporary; it will endure for all her life. Until the hour of her death she will be a mark for the scorn of the world—will be pointed at as the woman who married her uncle's servant. Can you realise what that means? I think not: but probably you can form some idea. however slight. it is bad enough when a man makes an unequal marriage and chains himself to an inferior; but for the woman who (low

div.head: CHAPTER XVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVIII.

! Ralph remained for some minutes after the Earl had gone, his face buried in his hands; then he got up and looked around him vaguely, its a man looks who is realising that everything he holds dear in life has been torn from him.

I The sunlight seemed to mock him with its brightness; the word "degradation" rang in his ears. Yes, the Earl had spoken the truth. He would have degraded her, dragged her down to his own level. And there was no hope. In that thought lay his greatest misery. He had spoken of 'making his way," "winning a fortune " ; but even as he had uttered the , words he knew that they were futile. Do what he would, he could never be worthy of her; he would still be Ralph Farringdon, the cow- • boy, the digger, the gamekeeper. Even if he succeeded in gaining a fortune—and fortunes are not easily gained nowadays—he would never be her equal in position. He had lost her for ever; but the madness of his love would remain while life lasted.

, He went out of the arbour, putting up ,his hand to ward off the sunlight as if it blinded him, and aimlessly wandered through the woods ,he had learnt to love—principally because she had passed through them. It was nightfall when he reached the hut, and at once he began to make up a small bundle from his box. While he was doing so, Burchett came in. Ralph looked round at him, and Burchett saw the pale and haggard face. "What is' the matter ? " he asked, curtly. "I am going," said Ralph. "Going? Why ? " demanded Burchett. • Ralph shook his head. "Don't ask me. I can't tell you." , _ . _ _

I "Something has happened ? " ' "Yes, something has happened," assented Ralph, with a bitter smile. "Something that renders it impossible for me to remain at Lynne Court any longer. Don't ask me. Let me go without a word. I'm sorry, but—but there is no help for it. It's not safe for me to stay here." "Not safe! But I ask no unwelcome ques- tions," said Burchett. "A man knows his own business. But I'm sorry, lad. Is there anything I can do ?" Ralph shook his head again and sighed.

"Withing. There is no-thing anyone can do," he responded. "I am going to start presently. I have made up a bundle of the things I must take and can carry. You'll let the rest stay until I send for them—it may be a long day, perhaps; never, I think." Burehett nodded, and stood watching him for a moment, then he drew out his old leather purse and laid it on the table. "Your wages,' he said. Ralph examined the contents. "There is more than's due to me," he said. "Take it." ejaculated Burchett.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Marquis of Granby's Coming of Age.—There are to be great rejoicings at Belvoir, to celebrate the coming of age of the Marquis of Granby, the only son of the Duke and Duchess of Rutland. The Derbyshire tenantry of the Duke are to be entertained on. the 24th of this month, when about 2,000 guests are to assemble for tea and festivities, and there will be a large house party ane entertainments at the Castle. The Duke and Duchess of Rutland have three daughters, of whom the two elder ones are out. Lady Marjorie and Lady Violet Manners, who, like their mother, are great favourites in Society. Their younger sister Lady Diana Manners, is some years younger, and is still in the schoolroom. Lady Marjorie Manners is a great personal friend of Princess Patricia of Connaught, and also of the young Queen of Spain, for whom the Duke and Duchess of Rutland gave a great ball in London just before her marriage last year. Royal Visit to Welbeck Abbey.—The King and Queen of Spain are to be the guests of the Duke and Duchess of Portland at Welbeck Abbey during their Majesties forthcoming visit to this country—and included in the house party invited to meet them will be the Duke and Duchess of Rutland and their daughters. The Duchess of Rutland, when Lady Granby, was one of the origina- tors of the remarkable Society known as the" Souls," and another of the original members was Miss Margot Tennant, now Mrs. Asquith. The Duchess of Portland was one of the later members, but the Society has since very nearly expired, owing it would seem, to the want of some definite object to live for. The Duchess of Portland who is entirely of Scottish lineage, is one of those leaders of Society who are always actively engaged in some or other useful cause, and sets her face against the playing of Bridge for high stakes. If cares are played at Welbeck it is recognised and understood by the guests that the stakes must be of quite a secondary consideration. Helping the Workers.—The Technical School estab- lished by the Duchess of Sutherland at Golspie apnears to have met with a larger measure of success than Lady Warwick's Secondary and Agricultural School at Dun- mow, which has been closed for want of pupils and financial support. The Sutherland Technical School was founded by the Duchess of Sutherland, three years ago, and a bazaar was held at Dunrobin Castle last week, to provide funds to assist the boys during their apprenticeship, after the three years course at the school. The Duchess of Sutherland is one of the best known of the many Society women, whose lives touch many interests, but perhaps one of the most practical schemes for helping forward the world, is the fruit- bottling and jam factory, established by Lidy Algernon Gordon-Lennox, at Broughton. The works which have been fitted up with all the most up-to-date appliances, and are run on business liner, promise to be a practical success, and not only save waste by using up to the best advantage to all concerned the produce of local fruit gromers, but also find regular employment for a large number of girls drawn from the Banbury district. Threatening the Bachelors.—History records many suggestions for the suppression of the bachelor, but although he is the subject of one of the oldest and most constant of social problems, the bachelor never flourished more than in the present day, and was never less inclined to be lured from his snug security. He laughs to scorn the idea of being taxed for the relief of those whose lives are burdened with numerous olive branches, but the rising tide of Socialism threatens to turn many things topsy-turvy, and it is possible that the idea may come to be regarded as not quite so ridicu- lous as he imagines it to be. Seeing however, that women have to a large extent wrested from men the means of livelihood, the latest idea is scarcely likely to meet with much support. This is, that spinsters should not wait until the age of sixty, or sixty-five, for old age pensions, but that they should have them at forty. It is of course,easy to plan out universal pension schemes, if you leave others the not unimportant part of finding the money, but in this case, it is suggested that the means to provide the spinster pensions should be found by a special tax on all bachelors. The idea will no doubt commend itself generally to women, although it will not find much favour among men, but however impractical it may seem to put into practice, there would certainly be a good dial of public support forth- coming, for measures to compel the bachelor to bear a more equal share of the burdens of the community. Teaching Simple Housekeeping.—Of late years, the County Councils and School Boards have done some- thing to educate the working classes in the arts of simple cooking and housekeeping, but the number of people they reach is comparatively small, and the League of Home Economics, which is an American institution, might well find its counterpart in similar organisations in London and the large provincial towns. The great majority of people live in the groove in which they are brought up. Their ways are the ways of the class to which they belong, and beyond that they give little thought to their diet, or the improved methods of preparing it. The American plan is not to ask the people to attend a school, but to send out women teachers to the large tenement houses, where the kitchen of one of the tenants is borrowed, and with what utensils and facilities it affords, to demonstrate I the most advantageous methods in purchasing supplies. I the cooking of meals, the feeding of children, and so' on. The lessons are made as personal as possible, and are attended by many of the inmates who would never think of going to school. In this way much is done to spread a better knowledge of simple housekeeping eshieh is not no well or generally understood in this

"Tabe it, or you'll offend me. You'll want money wherever you're going. And I've no use for it." There were ten sovereigns and some silver in the 1 urse. Ralph took out five pounds and was about to return the purse, but, changing his mind, put the balance of the money on the table, and the purse in his pocket. "I'll keep this if you'll let me, .se said. "It will remind me of all your kindness to me—pot Vint I shall want reminding. I shan't forget' it, Mr. Burchett."
H' turned away to fasten the bundle and to i hithe the misery n his eyes; then he looked round the room.

"There was a knife, an old friend-" he said. "I used it to cut some tobacco this morning," said Burchett. He took from the mantelshelf a long clasp knife with a ,alack horn handle, with filo initials "R. F." on it, and handed it to Ralph, who opened and shut it mechanically. "It is a very old friend," he said. have been sorry to leave it behind. give it to you if you'll, have it." -Burchett shook his head. "You'll want it, lat 3," he said.
"I should No! I will

lislph took a small gold pin of little worth from his scarf. "I'd like you to have that," ho snid simply; and as simply Burehett accepted it. "You look tired out," he said. "You will have something to eat and 'drink before you go 9 --

I'm tired," said ILalph. °l've had a ' time--" He checked himself. Not even to Lureliett could he hint of his trouble. "I shall ; b 4, all right when I get out of this place—though I }-lAnxen knows I have been happier here than I lave ever been in all my life!" Durchott made some tea and put it with some food on the table, and Ralph sat down. ire drank a cup of tea, but he could not eat, and he ,at with his head resting on his hand, staring at the lire as if he were lost in gloomy thought. 13urehett did not break the silence for some time, but at last he said in a low voice: "I suppose I can ask where you're goiog ? " nilph started as if from a dream, and rbse with a heavy sigh. -"Back to Australia, I fancy, but made no decided plans yet. There hasn't been time. I'll start now, I think." He thrust P. - stick through the handle of the bundle and hela out his hand.
"Good-bye," he said, hoarsely. Burchett gripped his hand—it was burning hot and quivering—and looked grimly into Ralph's fare.

"I'm sorry to lose you, lad," he said, gruffly. "I've grown used to you. But if you must go, you must; I've no right to keep you. Life's made up of partings." He sighed, dropped Ralph's hand, and turned to the fire. As Ralph went out he turned and looked back at the cosy room, the grim, bent figure, then he strode away with a heavy and weary step. The dogs followed him, whining, and he paused a moment to pat them and send them back.

The moon had not yet risen, but the night was clear and light, and he took the narrow path across the woods towards the high road. At a spot in the road from which he could catch a glimpse of the Court he stopped, and leaning against a tree looked long and yearningly at the great house—the casket that held his treasure. Treasure indeed! Gem fit for a King's crown, and not to be worn in the fustian jacket of a gamekeeper. As he stood there a slim, girlish figttre was passing at the turn in•the road. It was Fanny Mason. She happened to glance in his direction and saw him. She stopped and looked ,—as longingly as he was looking at the Court— then took a step towards him; but her feet were arrested by the sound of others. A nun was lurching along the road, coming from the opposite direction. It was the tramp. She saw him stop at sight of the tall figure by the ties and heard him address Ralph with a tipsy insolence.
"What—what are you a-stargazing at, my young spark ? " he said, with a leer. Ralph thus roughly awakened, looked at him and was passing on; but Oatway stretched out a hand and laid it on his arm.

"What's your hurry?" he demanded, wagging his head at him with exaggerated gravity of semi-intoxication.. "Looks as if you was a-goin' On a journey, swelp me ! " "Mind your own business, my man, and take your hand off my arm," said Ralph, quietly enough; and he shook the hand off. - "Oh, we're hoity toity, are we ? " jeered Oat- way. "We think we're somebody, don't we? Goin' a journey, eh? Got your bundle on yer back jes like a common tramp! Why "—with a- sudden laugh of insolent triumph—"hang me, if I don't think you've got the sack!" He peered into Ralph's face with eager, wolfish curiosity. "That's right enough! I can see it in your face! You'ive got the sack—been kicked out ! " His voice rose gloatingly, and he snapped his fingers in Ralph's face. "It's ups and downs with us, mister. You was up the other day and I was down; but its wicey wersey now, and I'm on the top—higher on top than you've a notion of, my young cockerel ! " Ralph had walked on, the man following him. But suddenly Ralph turned, and Fanny saw the white, haggard face plainly. She was frightened and waited for no more, but ran on, stopping at the end of the road which she expected Ralph to pass presently. Ralph looked at the man steadily but not angrily; his heart was too sore for him to be angered with the fellow. ‘Go your way, my man, and let me go mine", he said; but, as Oatway still seemed inclined to bother him, he left the road and entered the wood. Oatway, with a laugh of drunken audacity, followed him; but Ralph walked quickly, and Oatway presently gave up the aimless pursuit. Seating himself on a tree to get his breath, he drew out his pipe, and after -several ineffectual attempts lit it. . . . .

"He's goin',' he muttered with portentoun gravity and a would-be cunning leer. "Now what does that mean ? Hash the other fellow been up to any tricks, hash he been a-gettin' at him? If I thought so—if I thought as there'd been any underhand work—swelp me, I'd step in an' interfere! What did he say to-morrow night for, why not to-night? This 'ere game's a payin' one, and I'm goin' to play it for all it's worth, and I ain't goin' to be interfered with. I don't know as I want that young chap out o' my sight—though I hate him, hate him! Seems to me that I'd better see about it. I will too ! "

He rose unsteadily, but sank down again, began to yawn, and very soon fell asleep. Ralph went on his way. Presently the bundle struck against a tree. His stick was too long for its purpose, and he took out his knife to shorten it. As he was doing so the knife fell from his hand, struck his boot, and bounced to some distance. Ralph searched for it, but the under- growth was thick, and though he groped in the darkness he could not find the knife. He knew that he might grope till morning, and at last, with a sigh, he gave up the search. "Burchett might as well have had it," he said to himself as he left the spot. "It was the oldes friend I had."
Fanny waited at the corner for some time, but she concluded that Ralph had gone through the wood, and, being afraid to linger longer lest Oat- way should see her, she went reluctantly home- wards.

div.head: CHAPTER XIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XIX.
While the tragic act in the drama of two lives was being enacted in the arbour, Talbot Denby was shut up in his own room trying to face the knowledge which had come to him from Jim Oatway.

; Even yet he could scarcely bring himself to . believe in the man's statement, in the fact tha.. this gamekeeper fellow was the Earl's son and heir. But he knew that the thing would have to be faced, that he must either set at defiance this man who possessed the secret, or make terms with him. Make terms with a man who would probably blackmail him for the rest of his life ! He thought of a dozen plans for circumventing the man, of rendering the identification of Ralph Farringdon impossible; but one and all had to be discatded as impr, eticable. There seemed only one way, and th t was to submit to the blackmailing. Confuse and bewildered by Oa terrible problem, he pa dup and down the room, until it was time to dre for dinner. He had left his man in town, for the silent Gibbon was not a favourite with the Court servants, who were a sociable crew, and eyed the taciturn Gibbon with a kind of uneasy suspicion; and Talbot, on his visits to the Court, either availed himself of the services of the Earl s man, or was valeted by an intelligent young footman. He was therefore surprised, and in this over- wrought condition startled, when. in answer to his ring, lT11)001i iiims,ir appeared in the doorway, with his expressionless fivee and downcast eyes. IYou here! W.ll ?" ' said Talbot, with the ~old insolence which is Harder to bear than overt In utality.

Gibbon raised his eyes and held out a letter. It came this morning, sir, and as it was marked 'important and immediate,' I thought I'd better come down with it." 7 Talbot took the letter and opened it. It was from a famous moneylender, and its peremptory contents made Talbot's face grow even darker than it had been. "I wish to Heaven you would obey my orderg and remain where you are until you are sent for! The thing's of no consequence," he said, not angrily but with the same cold insolence. Gibbon dropped his eyes; they had been scanning his master's face while the latter had been reading. "Beg pardon, sir," he said in his toneiegti voice.

Then he put down the dress clothes he had on his arm, and proceeded to change his master's things as if the rebuke had passed over him unnoticed; but every now and then, as he per- formed his duty with noiseless assiduity, he glanced at the reflection of the dark face in the glass, and his white lids dropped still lower over his dull-looking eyes. "You'll have to remain till the morning," said Talbot, coldly, as Gibbon stepped back, his task accomplished. "You don't appear to be very welcome to the other servants, I hear, and I am not surprised. That hang-dog face of yours would convict you any day. I wonder sometimes why I endure it. Take yourself off by the first train, and don't come here again unless I send for you." • "Yes sir," resminded Gibbon, in exactly the same timeless voit% and unmoved manner' and he stood with meekly bowed head until hiEf master had left the room. Then his manner

changed swiftly, a spot of red started into his •'pale cheeks, his colourless eyes shone with an unwholesome light, and his teeth came together as if he were keeping back an oath. He wenb quickly to the letter which Talbot had crushed in his hand and flung it from him, and spreading it out he was reading it eagerly when he heard Talbot's returning step. He squeezed up tbsi letter and dropped it on the spot in which if had lain, and busied himself with the tweed suit. "The letter ? " said Talbot. Gibbon looked about him with dutiful alacrity, and Talbot picked up the letter and left the room. "It wasn't that," muttered Gibbon, musingly. "It wasn't that, serious as it is. He was look- ing bad before, when I came in. What is it? What is it, I wonder? He's in a tighter place than usual—l've never seen him skew the white feather before. What is it ? " He went over all the pockets in the tweed suit, searched the room in his stealthy, noiseless fashion, but though nothing rewarded him he was still unsatisfied.
"There was a desperate look in that faee of his," he muttered. .."I've watched him all these
months, like a cat does a mouse, but I've never seen him look so bad. He's too sharp as a rule, but to-night he looked as if—as if .he was hard .. ..

drove. For all his sharpness, I'll find it out. 'Hang-dog face!' Hang-dog face ! ' You little think, Mr. Talbot Denby, when you're speaking to me and treating me like a dog, how often feel like hanging for you." Talbot fdand the drawing-room empty. ._ _

"His lordship dines in his own roiini to-night, sir," said the butler; "and Miss Denby has a headache, and begs you will excuse her." Talbot inclined his head and checked a sigh of relief. He was in no mood for company thiri evening, for he knew that, admirable actor as hi. was it would be difficult to assume a light and easeful manner under the keen eyes of the old lord, and the cold, violet ones of Veronica. He made a pretence of eating some of the innumerable dishes, but his throat felt dry, and every morsel was a burden to him. But the wine was welcome, and he not only let the servants fill his glass repeatedly, but drank draught after draught of the claret when they had gone. There was a small caraffe of liqueur brandy on the table, and he finished up with that. The liqueur set his blood moving—he had felt cold ever since he had heard Oatway's story— and he rose with a flushed face and a kind of fever in his veins. He felt a desire to meet the man again, at once, to grapple with him, set his keen wits against the fellow's dull ones. Why had he made the appointment for to-morrow instead of to-night; why had he left the ruffian time to babble in his drink? Would it not be possible to see him to-night? He went upstairs to his room after a while, ,his mind still full of his desire to end his suspense, to meet Oatway and come to terms with him at once. Gibbon was in the adjoin- ing room, and heard his master pacing up and down; glen suddenly the sound of the restless footsteps ceased, and Gibbon, peeping through the keyhole, saw Talbot put on an overcoat, turn up the collar, and, with a cap drawn well ova his face, go to the door and look out. It was a time when all the servants were usually in their own part of the huge house, and Talbot, geeing the way clear, went down quietly and let himself out by the door of the back hall. Gibbon waited for a few minutes, then, slipping downstairs, caught up his own coat and hat, and, like his master, turning up the collar and drawing down the cap, followed stealthily. Talbot went through the shrubbery, pausing moment or two to listen, Gibbon pausing also; then, skirting the lawn, walked quickly along the fence that divided the park from the road, presently passed into the road through the small gate,and,after stopping to light a cigar, sauntered along it, as if he were taking an after-dinner stroll. S _

The night had grown rather cloudy, and the moon was obscured at times. Suddenly Gibbon caught the smell of rank tobacco coming from the wood on the left. His master had evidently also noticed it, for he stopped, and, with a cautious glance round, vaulted the fence and entered the wood. Gibbon, stealthily slipping from tree to tree, followed, his light grey eyes blinking like a ferret's, his lips hanging loosely like a blood. hound' a.

div.head: GIRL AT THE CONDITII
div.p: GIRL AT THE CONDITII
[ALL RIGHTS IES/1117ED.]
BY ALBERT LEE,
Author of "The Frown of Majesty," "The Go; aleman Pensioner," "King Stork of the Netherlands," "The Baronet in Corduroy," &o,

It WPS one of those burning_ hot.days when it was difficult to breathe, and when one longed to 'held out the open palms of one's hands in the hope of g.ting a chance -I‘llll of cool air •to lessen t e Heat. Dogs sat on the shady side of the 1--. Net and panted, feeling it too much exertion • ...Amble about the doings of their fellows in Cle canine world, while foot-passengers, if they emerged from a shady byway, crossed to the pavement where there was no sun. Even the horse that drew the water-em t which snlaked its lukewarm water on the stones went lazily, and the driver had not the 'energy to crack, his whip to makethe animal go faster. For what did it matter? Movement was a worry; so was theught, and the only good of life just then was to find a spot where one could be cool. It was hot everywhere —in town and country, on the road and by the riverside., None would envy the cyclist on such a day, when the sun seemed to burn itself into the very walls of the churches and warehouses, or put more glowing colour into the scarlet poppies in the cornfield.

There passed down Bouverie-street in the hottest part of that hot afternoon one whose , dress and general bearing bespoke the gentle- man. His face was so handsome, that had it been a cooler day the women would have taken the trouble to look at him and pass on with a plea,ant wonder as to what woman would be made happy by his love, or have the privilege of :being his wife. But he gave no one the im- pression that he was conscious of the power which good looks possess. He went on as others did, slowly, feeling the heat too great for him ito carry his black, silver-mounted ebony stick Cs, his hand, but holding it under his arm to Jake the burden seem so much less. Presently he came to a standstill, for half-a- dozen wayfarers, glad for any excuse to stay the toil of movement, were grouped before one of the conduits from which, in olden days, before : water companies came into existence, the people , of the neighbourhood obtained water for drinking . and domestic purposes. The tap was large, and was fixed in an alcove in the wall of one of the !City churches, so that when the iron bar was ! pulled forward, it set the water free, and allowed it to splash refreshingly in the hollowed stone beneath.

The bystanders, however, were not concerned with the tap and the water that poured from it, but with two girls who sat on either side in the alcove, and were performing their ablutions in the most nonchalant manner. As they sat, Turkish fashion, on the stones, one saw their wets bare arms, and envied their coolness. One of the girls was very beautiful, the other plain; but both were so dressed that the way- farer would say to himself that they were very poor. The linen which shewed at their open necks was torn, and by no means spotless, and the skirts were ragged round the bottom edges, to say nothing of rents. As for sleeves, they were so short that the elbows and most of the upper arm were bare. They sat on, indifferent to the loiterers, and, having dried their arms and hands and faces, -Int on with, their toilet, which was aided by use of a broken pietce of looking-glass, combs which were minus many of their teeth, and two dirty pieces of ribbon with which to tie up the hair. The comb had evidently been snapped in two, so as to do duty for two heads at one and the same time. The girls were in no wise em- barrassed, for now and again one would say something to the other in a low voice, and look- ing at the bystanders they laughed, then drew their combs through their long hair with greater deliberation.

The handsome stranger halted merely because the way was blocked by the loiterers, and the sudden stoppage of his progress caused him to Look up as if to find a cause. Then he saw these girls, and gazed at them in surprise. They were Just now gathering together their paraphernalia and carefully putting them away in their pockets. The nearest girl was a beautiful blonde, and as she put forth her hand, so that a portion of the upper arm was uncovered, she tdisplayed a strange pale-blue device which someone had tattooed there. lt,was of considerable size and conspicuous—as large as the top of a tea-cup, and encircled with a round and ornamental border.

None of the idle spectators took notice of this. Perhaps they counted it an ordinary thing among the poor in a seaport city; hut the new- comer saw it and started. Involuntarily he bent Invard and looked at it curiously, then said ..vmething beneath his breath, and looked again.

The girl glanced up and saw the stiange expression on his face, and marking how hand- some he was, and how eagerly he gazed, her own face flushed a rosy red, which spread to her neck and arms. As if her modesty had been suddenly awakened she drew her bodice together tightly, and fastened such buttons as were on the broken garment, and only glanced at him again surrep- titiously. Then she rose to her feet and moved away, followed by the other girl, who had watched her keenly, and saw the blush with some amuse- ment.

Oblivious to the looks and nudge q of the by- standers, the stranger gazed after the two girls who sauntered away idly, and, crossing &the road into the broiling sun, turned down a side street and disappeared. Then he went forward just as slowly, and followed them. • . _ _
Ode- woman's elbow went into the side of a neighbour, and when she had attracted her attention she shook her head.
"Those girls are not for the likes of him," she said.
"No," came the answer; "but he thinks of that handsome Bryony. Isn't that what .they call her ?

"Ic,s. She's right enough for all that I can tell; hut when these gents are attracted by such a face there's no good meant. Come along." The two women walked a yard or two, but 1-..:sed again to look after_ the stranger, who presently- went rould the street corner and was no more seen.

The stranger, whose name was Clarence Roget, contented himself with looking at the house into which the two girls entered, then making a note of the number, and the name of the narrow line, he went about the business he had on liana]. But throughout the day he was taciturn, and going to his hotel, v hieh faced the river, he took a table at the window and ate his dinner in silence. There were not many in the great dining-hall, so that he had, the little table to himself, and, far from troubling as to what was going, simply ate what the waiter brought him. The man looked at him again and again in, surprise, for Clarence was usually a hearty eater, enjoying his meals, and taking an interest in what was going; but now he ate listlessly, or left the plate untouched, and whenever spoken to by the waiter as to his wishes, merely answered in monosyllables. It was the same in the matter of taciturnity when he went to the smoking-room; he chose the quietest corner, wheeled the lounge chair round, and stared out of the open French window, through which came river sounds, the noise of the bells of the electric trams, and the laughter of courting couples, or the sedater tramp of men and women who had business on hand, and went

with what speed the hot evening allowed. .c.ven his cigar was forgotten, for it went out, and finally fell from between his fingers and lay unnoticed among its ashes on the carpet. "Can it be possible ?" he said to himself presently. "Twas a beautiful face—fat and away too beautiful for one in such a position. But as for that tattoo mark, it is what my. uncle told me of. I was to search and sea&h for that, and on a girl's arm in this city; to search until I found it, and if I pro,secuted the search I rhould hear of something to my advantage. Let me think what else he said. It was the tattoo mark of two doves face to face, one perching on a box, the other holding a key in its mouth. 'And read well among the devices that make the border,' he said, by way of conclusion." Clarence pauised. and bending down Dial:pi-1 nu

_— memory ana Jove age wnen sne saw tnarenee. She knew his pride, that he would never ask her to be his wife lest it should be thought that he sought her fortune to swell his own. But that he loved her she knew well. She waited, but he did not speak; and the delay was painful. One day she saw him in the bower while she was talking in the drawing-room with Mrs. Tillotson. She asked to be excused, and went into the garden, where for a time she walked to and fro irresolutely. At last she went to the bower. "Clarence," she said. ,"Yes, Bryony." He always called her by that name. "You love me, do you not?" "Heaven only knows how much, my darling!" "Then why do you not ask me to be your wife ? " He sprang to his feet, and, taking her hand in his, put his question: "Will you ? "
ITHE END. 1

div.head: TERRIBLE TRACEDY AT WIDNES. 18 Workmen in the Canal.
div.p: TERRIBLE TRACEDY AT WIDNES. 18 Workmen in the Canal.
THREE DROWNED

At one o'clock on Thursday a shocking drowning tragedy occurred at Widnes ion the ferry near the Hutchinson works of the Uniteid Alkali Company. It is the practice of the men working at these works to be conveyed across the Sankey and St. Helens canal in a flat-bottomed boat known as" the coffin "because of its peculiar shape. At one o'clock on Thursday the men made a rush to board the boat as they are in the habit of doing, and eighteen crowded on board despite the fact that the maximum load was twelve. In this overcrowded state it was pushed Off, and when in mid-stream it sank. The men were thrown into the water, but assistance was promptly forthcoming. Their workmates on the bank threw ropes to them. and the majority were promptly rescued from their dangerous position. William Price. Alilton-street ; William Frodsham, and Fred Keratin. nu apprenticed plumber, sank. Their bodies were quickly recovered, and arti- fice' respiration was applied by Drs. Hodgkinson, and Edwards, who were soon on the spot, but life wits extinot.

At ten o'clock next morning a disagreeable I surprise was in store for him. He went to the nouse and stood at the door of Mrs. Padgett's room. No answer came to his repeated knocks, and having waited until he grew impatient he opened the door and looked in. The room was ; empty. Even the furniture, such as it was, was ' gone, and nothing remained but the frayed-edged , prints upon the walls. A woman was going downstairs at the time and she halted to stare at Clarence. She thought he was a doctor, and spoke. "They're gone." "So I see. But where ? " "Heaven only knows! I saw a man in the street early this morning piling up his truck with their bits o' things, and they went. That's all I know." Clarence, unable to obtain any information beyond that, went back to his hotel, feeling intensely disappointed. He found it hard to reconcile Brvonv's softness and tears with this disappearance. Ana, what was more, Beaty seemed to want money so badly that he thought she would not willingly forgo the nine sovereigns that were to come to her if she could discover anything in the border of the tattoo mark. The raore he thought of this. the more his , Wonder grew, but when evening came, and hi ' was sitting at the open window, as he had done the night before, and smoked, a new idea came to him. Mrs. Padgett was going to blackmail him. Perhaps during the night she had discovered something in the border, and meant to get money for it. He was looking down the street and saw a gir. loitering. Presently she beckoned to a gamin who was trying to earn a copper by turning wheels alongside a tramcar which had some holiday- makers on the top. The boy went to her, and she gave him something which he put into his pocket. She also put a piece of paper into his hand, and pointed to the hotel. Then she drew back and watched him. The boy came quickly, but halted when he got to the hotel and looked about him. He was fearful as to his reception if he ventured up the steps so that he stood, and hording an envelope at its corners between hie two forefinger tips, blew at it, and made it revolve at each blow on these dirty pivots. A thought came to him, and he peered towardt the window where Clarence sat, saw him there. and hurried to him. "Ain't you the gent wot give me a cigar ? " the gamin asked. "Yes." "Well, it was a jolly smoke. Wish I had another." Clarence made no offer in spite of the boy's looks towards the table. "What's your busi- ness ? " he asked instead. "I had to give this to a gent named Roget. Where shall I find him ? " the boy said, dis- appointed at Clarence's unwillingness to be generous. _ _

- "Well, I happen to be Mr. Roget." "Then take it," said the boy, handing him an envelope which was dirty and fingered, and crumpled by one who was not often employed to carry such missives. "Any answer ? " asked Clarence, taking the note. "Don't know. She said as she'd wait till I came back," the boy replied, pointing his thumb over his shoulder. Clarence tore open the envelope and found a well-written note on dirty paper, but that he cared not for. He was absorbed in the contents, which considerably astonished him. "Sir,—You shall see what is on Bryony's arm for a hundred pounds. I shall not take less. If you like, I will bring her to the hotel. We've )ooked at it, and there's something ,there that's worth your while, I expect. "MARY PADGETT. "
"Is the girl who gave you this in sight ?" asked Clarence of the boy who was staring at him intently. "Yes, guy'nor." "Then fetch her, and there's a shilling for you viiben she comes."

"I will make it worth your while, Mrs. Padgett. I will give you the hundred pounds in notes, is I promised Beaty, and another hundred to- morrow night, if I have such service from Bryony as she can render me." "Can't I render it ? " ".No."

V. At half-past ten on the following morning Clarence drove up to the door of the houst where Mrs. Padgett had taken fresh lodgings. Bryony came instmtly, for she had been watching for him at the window. She had seen this man, and it was like Heaven, she thought, to be in his company. Whatever he had asked of her she would have done it for his sake, and now that he only wanted such a simple thing of her as her company in a bank for a few minutes, just to shew her arm there, she felt sorry that the service was so slight. To her he looked so full of honour, so true a man, and so complete a gentleman, that she was convinced he would want nothing wrong of her. As they rode through the streets together, neither of them speaking more than an occasional word, she wondered who Clarence was. Then her memory—which had been blank, so Beaty had told her, ever since a dangerous illness—began to be active, and made the past assume shape , and form. She looked at her shabby dress, and !thought she could call to mind a time when she had been richly clothed. She had a vision of something which, by comparison with the squalor she had lived in for so long a time, was like a scene in fairyland. Bet, of course, it was all a dream—a dream of servants and luxury, of enjoyment and beauty, and all the sights and sounds and surroundings which she had seen the !ike of whenever she and Beaty ventured in these parts of the city where the wealthy dwelt. The dream went on. She remembered among this luxury a kind but eccentric man, who for many a morning stood by her and pricked her arm and slowly formed this strange device at which Clarence had been looking. He wore strong glasses when he worked with the needles which made her arm feel sore, but he would laugh and say at times that it would mean all manner of good things for her some day. Then the dream began to fade and darkness came upon her suddenly, and le never had any thought of that dream again until now, when she was sitting in the carriage with Roget. She sighed. "Why do you sigh ? " Clarence asked, looking i at her kindly. The ride was a long one, and touched by his I kindness and his lack of pride in riding with her I —he so richly dressed, and she so shabby—she told him this dream of hors which had ended in dp..rkness. But as she told the dream, and set it Thrth in greater detail now that she was speak- ing, and mentioned names and described places and people, he stared at her in amazement. It was so much like what he knew of, with this excep- tion—that she called it a dream, while he knew ' it all as terribly real. "Are you sure it Was a dream, Bryony ? " he asked, laying his hand on hers. "It could only be such," she answered, softly.

"Let me tell you ./ay dream," he said; and he set forth some of his own ex;.)eriences. As she looked him in the face, and watched his lips, her eyes widened, and a new light came into them. Where she had spoken somewhat roughly at the conduit, as one would do who had dwelt where the daily language and manners were foul and unseemly, she began to soften. She was no longer the rough, uneuitured girl who sat and laughed without shame at the conduit, and had naught but an accidental beauty to recommend her. She was the girl of culture, one with a rich softness of face and manner, one who, by an occasional word, spoke as they would speak who were gently born and were nurtured in affluence. We are reminded that there THE COMEDY is a Tariff Raform Corn- OF TARIFF mission still in existence. REFORM. The reminder takes the

form of a request for a donation from a firm which has supplied the Com- mission with information. Money is wanted to help in " popularising the results of the investi- gations." This intimation is reinforced by a letter from Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who, we are glad to &id, is well enough to write notes in favour of what he no doubt regards as the good cause, and accurately to remember his old formula. "The time is shortly coming," he says, " wlAen the people of this country will no longer be satisfied to'contribute toward the revenue of our competitors whilst these are allowed free access to our markets.' Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was always fond oi a phrophecy ; and certainly he has a right to vatieinate if he can see any indications of the speedy triumph of a Protectionist policy in the late General Election, or in the events that have since occurred. His method of stating he effects of a Protectionist tariff is worthy of the movement it is intended to assist. It conjures up the picture of the trading and manufacturing nations of the world paying each other taxes, and thus helping each other and themselves, after the manner of thcse communities who earned a precarious sub- sistence by taking in each other's washing. Another portion of Mr. CHAMBEIRLAIN'S letter sugg3sts that his friends do not keep him informed as to what is going on in the world outside High- bury. They can scarcely have enlightened him, for instance, concerning the recent changes in the Commonwealth Tariff, so vehemently protested agaeost by his own neighbours the members of the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce. If he had heard of Sir WILLIAM LYNIVB practical denorn- stration of the nature of a Tariff Reform ' policy he could hardly have written that the proceedings of the imperial Confer- ; enca have shown that we have no time to lose if W 3 would secure the rapidly-increasing trade which is offered to us by our kinsmen across the sea. We wish to speak with all respect of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, especially during the continuance of his present condition of health ; but we feel it to be our duty to say that the Imperial Conference has shown nothing of the kind. What it showed more clearly than anything else is that there are some level-headed Colonial Premiers, like Sir WILFRID LAURIER ; that the lother Country must be permitted to enjoy as much liberty as her Colonies, and to deal with her Fiscal affairs as if they were something exclusively her own ; and that there are others, like Mr. DEAKIN, who are not indisposed to play into Mr. CTIAMBERLA.IN'S hands, whilst also making trade between the Mother Country and the Colonies as difficult as possible. We are not being offered an increlsing trade by our kinsmen across the sea, if we exclude Canada from consideration. We are being offered a smaller trade carried on under increasing diffi- culties.

Simultaneously, with the :ppearance of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S letter comes a telegram from Melbourne stating that Mr. DEiKIN has decided to resist the pressure that is being used to induce him to abandon thh British preference. This is highly farcical. Mr. DRAKIN is pretending to do us a favour on the one hand, and on the other he is being pressed to equalise the tariff by building a wall equally high between the British and the foreign exporter. To put the case still more plainly, there is in Australia, at the very time that we are hearing so much about preferences, a strong party which desires to exclude Great Britain from the Australian markets. That is why S r WlLLiam LYNE has put five guineas on bicycles and t3a guineas on motor- bicycles. The intention is to exclude corn peting trade in the interests of Australian manufacturers. And this is what Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN describes ag offering us an increasing trade! There is another aspect of the question which is well worth the attention of those who have not yet quite made up their minds on the Tariff Reform question. Mr. DEAKIN is assailed not only by those who wish to keep the foreign 'producer out of the market, but still more fiercely by those who find that the new tariff has greatly raised the price of every article of consumption, and who, not being manufacturers, do not quite see why and for whose benefit. Will those who think it is the exporter who gains kindly tell us why, in that case, prices have gone up to the people of Australia, and what these increased prices are paying for?
We have no doubt our THE MEMBER. readers will be pleased to . _

learn that Mr: A. H. Crosfield, M.P., is thoroughly enjoying his holiday in Switzerland. After a heavy Parliamentary session, the Member for Warrinaton was, like many other Legislators, in need of both change of environment and rest. For the past two or three weeks he has been golfing at St. Moritz and

Lucerne and winning Increased popularity as the President of the Swiss Golf Association. Mr. Crosfield is not merely an ornamental figure-head; he is one of the most expert playing members and in the competitions last week he ran into the championship final and lowered the amateur record for the first part of the course. Then as President, Mr. Crosfield gave a dinner and a dance, both of which seem to have been enormously successful. While apparently having such an enviable time, Mr. Crosfield is by no means indifferent to politics and the trust reposed in him by his constituency. While staying at St. Moritz he has had the honour of entertaining the Chief Secretary for Ireland and Mrs. Birrell frequently, and has doubtless picked up some valuable Parliamentary and political points from the astute Me. Btrrell. there are few men who keep in such close touch with the administrative chiefs as does Mr. Crosfield, and the experience and knowledge he is thus gain- ing must eventually be of considerable) service in what we hope will be a lengthy Parliamentary career.
The need for Protection THE NEED FOR seems to be emphasized by PROTECTION, the sad state of affairs die-

closed by the balance sheet of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Limited. Under Free Trade, the Company can only make £110,680 profit on a capital of £860,000, and pay a miserable dividend of 10 per cent. on the ordinary shares. Coal has gone, and iron has gone, apparently I Yet most people would be able to extract a grain of satisfaction from such a report as the directors of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Limited have to present. Possibly these gentlemen are not altogether displeased though they are Protectionist to the core. This is almost the best year Messrs. Peamon and Knowles, Ltd., have had, and shows a big advance on any returns of recent date. In three years the profit has doubled itself, and the business of the concern is rapidly increasing. There is, presumably, good ground for anticipating even better things in the immediate future, for the balance sheet takes no account of profits on the working of Messrs.Rylands Bros.Ltd.,and the Moss Hall Collieries, both of which concerns have been recently purchased by the Pearson and Knowles Co. Ltd., and are doubtless enjoying an enviable prosperity. We very cordially congratulate the parent company on the handsome result of the mist year's trading, and trust that even under Free Trade this happy condition of affairs may continue. Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Ltd. are the biggest employers of labour in the town, and their success can only be a source of satisfaction to Warringtoa people. In the extent of their operations they bid fair ere long to rival the municipality itself, and at the same time show a better return for the money invested.

We are pleased to note that MEMORIAL TO THE measures are being REV, E. J. so promptly taken to WlLLcoms. raise a suitable memorial to the late Rev. E. J. Willcocks,headmaster of the Warrington Grammar School. It often happens that an effort of this kind is so delayed that the response from sympathisers is jeopardised. There can be no greater compliment to the memory of the dead than that a memorial should be raised at once,and it is a matter for great satisfaction that a scheme to perpetuate the memory of the late reverend gentleman should be already in shape. So far :it has not been possible to do more than appoint a representative Committee of subscribers and invite suggestions for the form of the memorial. The most suitable idea, and probably the one which would be most in accord with the views of so ardent an educationist as the late Mr. Willcocks, is that of founding a scholarship in his name, and we hope a great effort will be made to raise the necessary capital sum for the purpose. There seems to us no comparison in reason between founding a scholarship or prize, and building a chancel for the new Church at Orford, as was sug- gested. This would be a good thing for Orford, but as a memorial to Mr. Willeocks it would be lacking altogether in utility, and very much in appropriateness.

Mr. C. H. M. Wharton, the THE WORKINGMAN newly-appointed revising AND HIS VOTE. barrister, has signalised the holding of his first Court at Warrington by an important pronouncement. Hitherto it has been the custom of the Revising Barrister to sanction claims which the party, agents agreed should be allowed, without insist- ing upon evidence in support. In future, how- ever, this formal procedure will be forbidden. Mr. Wharton will require every claim presented for his approval to be borne 3ut by some kind of proof. Mr. Howes pointed out that the desire of the agents was to study the convenience of the workingman to whom absence from work for any reason often means serious loss. The Revising Barrister appeared to be convinced of the unreasonableness of expecting the claimant in every case to attend, but suggested that his representative might come, adding that the franchise was important and "either it was worth looking after or it was not." At length he declared that if an agreement or rent book were produced, that would be sufficient. The decision will have far- reaching effects, and will make the obtaining of a vote a still more difficult process. The law on the question is bad enough in all conscience, for the citizen has often to be prepared to suffer much inconvenience and badgering before securing what should be his birth-right. It should be the aim of those who administer the law to make it as easy as possible for people to obtain the franchise—the only lever which the majority have to enable them to play their part in shaping the destinies of the country.

The man who contemplates OLD-Aaz PENSIONS, the subject of Old-Age Pensions may reasonably contemplate it with hope. The Government is likely to give them, and of the proportion who are likely to live to sixty-five the experience of the Mancheste7 Unity of Oddfellows—the friendly society holding first rank—may be called in evidence. Their books show that of 100,000 persons of the age of sixteen years 54,006 live to be sixty-five, and the average outlook from that point adds five years to the promise of the Psalm- ist. On an average, those who see sixty-five live to be seventy-five. This doubtless refers to a good type of life. Over 40,700 live to be seventy. It is interesting to note, while , national old-age pensions are under discus- sion, that the Foresters have lately made the first Idefinite movement in the history of friendly socie- ties towards supplying such pensions to their members. At the last High Court a resolution instructed the Executive Council to formulate a scheme for compulsory payment against the claims of old age of every new entrant. This is a drastic proposal. The payment is to ensure 53, a week at seventy in lieu of sick-pay there- after. At present on the endowment insurance 1 rates a member joining at thirty-five might pay £3 a year in addition to his annual subscrip- tion, and receive £lOO down at sixty-five. This is obviously not the same thing as 4d. a week for all and sundry, according to Lord Avebury's plan. Some of the local districts of Oddfellows provide 53. a week in case of old age, but no general scheme exists to-day by which a thrifty man may do as well for himself as the Government scheme may not bb so much as surmised. One thing is certain, there is plenty of scope for Mr. Asquith's ingenuity and enterprise.

The Wesleyans of Warrington are delighted with their new minister, the Rev. Thomas Miller, who possesses no mean pulpit powers and who has already gained a reputation as a diligent "visitor." Mr. Miller, too, appears to be favourably impressed with Warrington and at his recognition meeting on Thursday said that not m%ny industrial towns would equal it in beauty. We must be progressing rapidly towards the" Beautiful Warrington ' ideal * *

One of our Tory-owned contemporaries the " Obsrver," indulged in a little feeble sarcasm at the expense of Mr. Crosfield the other day. They remarked: "We think Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, the member for Warrington, Ival have spent a very happy week golfing at Interlaken, Switzerland, in marked contrast to the spirit in which he appears to carry out his Parliamentary duties." Unfortunately for the " Observer's" little joke, their continental detective was wrong in his facts. Mr. Crosfield was. not at Interlaken at all, and did not attend the championship meeting there. * * * RESOLUTIONS OF THE HAGUE CONFERENCE.

As might be expected, many incumbents are show - ing a determination to result against the "leading rein " or the Bishops in reference to the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. The Rev. H. F. Tracey, vicar of Dartmouth, has posted a copy of his bishop's prohibi- tion of the celebration of deceased wife's sister marriages by his clergy communication in the Church porch, but has appended the following note : I think it right to say, in connection with the above, that with every respect for the bishop's wishes I feel bound to be guided rather by what is now the law of the land—in other words, I should not hesitate to marry those whom the law of the land declares eligible. o ec What is wisdom but having a great deal to say and keeping silent ?--FRANKFORT MOORE.
