If a child in a house is a well-spring of pleasure, then a child on a boat is nothing less than a water-, spout. —EDE. Better vote for an efficient devil that knows his own mind and his own business than for a foolish patriot who has no mind and no business. -G. BEIZICIRD SHAW. • The motoring correspondent of the " Dispatch " has something to say this week about a familiar road danger—the " monkey-backed " bridge. He says : "I have twice in this column called attention to these in general, and in particularly mentioned the one just beyond Lymm, on the Warrington road. This spans a canal, and is only sufficiently wide for one vehicle, with very steep gradients on either side near the apex. Some day there will be a terrible smash there if two cars meet, as nothing can be seen from either side until the top is reached. A few days ago I rushed up from the Warrington-Thelwall side to dis- cover when on the apex another car not ten yards away making for the top. The driver looked scared, and a lady passenger grasped his arm in evident alarm. Fortunately the road widens on each side of the bridge, and they gave me all the room possible, and I glided by. Had I been two seconds later, or they two seconds earlier, disaster could not have been avoided. In the interetts of public safety the bridge should be widened without delay.

* 00 At the last meeting of the Education Committee there was a lengthy discussion on the obvious hard- ship on pupil teachers who had failed to secure admission to the training colleges, owing to lack of accommodation. It will be remembered that the Committee, by the Cnairman's casting vote, decided to deduct from these teachers' salaries a sum equal to the loss of the Government grant. The question will be revived at the meeting on Monday next, when Mr. Edward Plinston will move :—" That, in the cases of those pupil teachers who, on the completion of their apprenticeships, have passed the Preliminary Examina- tion for the Certificate, but have, failed to secure admission into Training Colleges owing to the lack of accommodation in such Colleges, and whose engage- ments are extended by the Committee as half-time teachers, no deduction shall be made from their salaries because of the loss of the Government ',,rant, but that they shall be paid at the same rate as during the last year of their engagements."

A Parliamentary return issued on Monday gives a lurid glimpse of the poverty and privation existing in the wealthiest city in the world. During last year coroners' juries returned forty-eight verdicts of "Death from starvation" or" Death accelerated by privation" in the administrative County of London. The North-Eastern and Eastern Districts, containing parishes like Shoreditch, Bethnal Green, Whitechapel, Poplar, and Stepney, head the list NN ith 1,5 and cases respectively, the City of Westminster, which is the antithesis of East London, furnishing only one. The majority of the men and women were over fifty years of age, but inquests were held on an infant of four weeks, a labourer of twenty-eight, and women of twenty-nine and thirty years of age. The verdicts are painful reading. Disease accelerated by alcoholic excess, want of food, exposure, neglect, or lack of medical attendance accounted for most of the deaths. In many instances the victims were homeless wanderers with no occupation, but the list includes the widow of a piano manufacturer, the wife of a law clerk, a clerk, an ex-bandmaster of the Life Guards, and a crossing- sweeper.

div.head: LICENCEE PROSECUTED.
div.p: LICENCEE PROSECUTED.
The Sale of Drink to Children.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday before the Nlayor and other magistrates,Arthur Moffatt,licelasee of the British Tar Inn, was summoned for serving a child under the age of 14 years in an unsealed vessel.— Mr. F. G. Taylor represented defendant and pleaded not guilty. P.C. Lewis said at 9.20 p.m. on August 31st he was on duty near Stamford-street when he saw a little girl leave the British Tar with a bottle of beer(prodnced).on seeing him she ran away, but he stopped her, and asked her where she had got it from,and she replied,Nloffatt's. He asked how old she was, and she said she would be "fourteen to-morrow." Witness took the girl back to _Moffatt's, and Mrs. Moffatt admitted having served her, but said she did not know she was under age.

Sarah Davies said she was 12 years of age last Jane. Mrs. Moffatt served her with the beer and Mr. Robin- son sent her for it. She told Mr. Moffatt the first time she went that she was fourteen. Mrs. Moffatt was present at the time. Mr. Taylor said that a fter that evidence,he had no case to answer, as the ' girl had met the case for him. Mr. Moffatt had asked her if she was 14, and she said she was.

The Bench retired and on their return the Mayor said the case must go on. Mr. Taylor said there was no doubt they had supplied the beer, but they were under the impression that the girl was fourteen. The beer was served at a very busy time on Saturday night. The Bench again retired, and on their return the Mayor said they had taken the defendant's previous good character into consideration, and had decided to dismiss the case on payment of costs. Publicans ought to use very great care in serving children. Alban Robinson, forgeman, 18, Watkin-street, was summoned for sending the child for the beer, knowing her to be under the age of fourteen years. Defendant pleaded guilty. P.C. Lewis said he took the girl to Robinson's house, and he admitted sending her for the beer, and said he was to blame. At that time Robinson was drunk and had a bottle of beer at the side of him.
Defendant denied being drunk. He was not aware that she was under fonrteen. The Chief Constable said defendant han not been beforo the Court before. -
Defendant was fined 55., including costs.

On Saturday afternoon a little boy named William , Brady, aged seven years, son of James Brady,. 53, Oak- -land-street, had a narrow escape from drowning. He was playing by the water edge, close to the promenade with some other boys, and during the larking he fell in and was being swiftly carried away by the ebbing tide. Mr. Waring, of Oakland-street, and Sergeant-Major Lynch, a transporter bridge employ, at once saw the ,difficulty the boy was in. The former rushed into the water and was soon in difficulties himself, although be got hold of the lad. Sergeant Lynch went to their assistance, and brought both, in an exhausted condition, to the side. Artificial respiration was at once com- menced on the child and Mr. Wareing, and after both had been taken to the hospital they were taken home. At half-past four on Monday afternoon Captain Pyfleld, of the Runcorn and Widnes Grappling Corps, and Police-constable Rawcliffe recovered the body of Daniel Ford, of Pollock-street, Glasgow. from West Bank Dock. Deceased was a fireman on board the steamer Isleman, and had been missing since Saturday. Having no knowledge of his whereabouts, the dock was dragged, and the body was recovered at the time stated. THE INQUESTS. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquests on Tuesday. The first inquiry was into the cause of the death of Donald Ford, aged thirty-three years, a "fireman on board the steamship Salesman, of Glasgow. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." The second inquiry was into the death of Thomas Hooligan, the four-months-old son of Peter Hooligan, chemical labourer, Tingserley-street. The mother said the child had never looked up since its vaccination, and died on Saturday without a doctor seeing him. Dr. Hutchinson said he remembered vaccinating the child, but it had absolutely nothing to do with the child's death. A verdict of" Death from natural causes "was returned. HAYDOCE CLERGYMAN'S MARRIAGE. 'The chucchpeople of Haydock were greatly interested on Tuesday in the marriage of the Rev. Traverse S. Stoney, who for the past two and a half years has been in charge of the now parish of St. Mark's, Haydock. Mr. Stoney's marriage took place at Sidcup, Rent, in the church of which the Roy. Canon Bardsley, formerly vicar of Huddersfield, is vicar. The bride was Miss Bardsley, sister of the Rev. Cyril Bardsley, vicar of St. Helens, and she is well known and very popular in St. Helens, where she has worked in connection with her brother's parish for some time.

COLLIERY FATALITY AT HAYDOCK. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Haydock on Tuesday, an the body of James Holland, aged GO, of 58, Ramford-street, St. Helens, who was fatally injured at the No. 5 pit, Southport Colliery, and died from his injuries in the Haydock Hospital.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: Y.M.C.A. ENTERTAINED.
div.p: Y.M.C.A. ENTERTAINED.

At the invitation of their President, Colonel Richard Pilkington, C. 8., about 200 members of the local Y.M.C.A. on Saturday, journeyed by special train to St. Helens, where they were joined by other branches of the Y.M.C.A. of the surrounding districts. The beautiful grounds and gardens of Rainford Hall are just now at their best, and the visit was greatly enjoyed. A friendly cricket match, got up between the branches, resulted in a victory for the St. Helens branch. After tea short addresses were given,aud Mr. Profit, otEarles-1 town, said the bond whibh existed between the dis- tricts, was due to the great interest taken by their President and his family, in everything connected with the welfare of the Y.M.C.A (Applause.) Colonel Pilkington, in addressing his guests, said be was delighted to see so many present. Nothing gave him greater pleasure than to see so many young people about him enjoying themselves.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 14, 1907.
WARRINGTON

Coming Events. The first rehearsal of the season in connection with eh* Musical Society will be held in the Cairo-street schoolroom on Tuesday evening at 7.30. Intending new members should meet the conductor at 7 o'clock. Elgar's" Dream of Gerontius " is the work for practice. There will be a joint Liberal picnic to Belle Vue on Saturday next. Trains will leave Warrington Central at 1 and 2 p.m..returning at 10 and 10.15 p.m. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. will accompany the party and deliver an address in the grounds. Tickets, includ- ing admission to grounds, tea and firework display,are Is. 9d. each, and can be obtained from lir. J. Howes jun., Liberal Club. WHITE TOASTING CFIRESE,6d. per lb.at ASHLEY'S.—Advt. Stockton Heath Recreation Ground. At a meeting of the Parish Council on Tuesday evening the question of a recreation ground was dis- cussed, and it was decided to hold a Parish meeting on Tuesday, October 15th. Education Committee. The usual monthly meeting of the Education Committee will be held in the Town Hall on Monday evening at 6 o'clock. ' •

KEIL BUTTER, is. per Ib.—ASIILF,Y'S, Sankey st.—Advt Price of Bread. The Warrington Master Bakers' and Confectioners' Association announce an advance in the price of bread of one half-penny per 41b. loaf, commen3ing on Monday next.

Taxation of Land Values. The last excursion of the Warrinaton Branch of the English League for the Taxation of Land Values took place on Saturday last to the "Childs of Hale." It was decided to hold the first annual meeting of the League on Friday, October 11th.

Personal. The Rev. A. S. Cameron, M.A.' vicar of Weston St. Mary's, Spalding, and formerly curate at the Warrington Parish Church, has been appointed Diocesan Inspector of Schools for the Deanery of East Elloe.

SPLENDID PURE Bu .112ER,10c1. per lb.at ASHLEY'S.—Advt Mr. C. Toft's Achievements. The 50 Guinea Silver Challenge Cup offered for annual competition at the Bakers' and Confectioners' Exhibi- tion held in the Agricultural Hall, London, this week, for the best collection of bread has again been awarded to Mr. Toft, of Warrington. This is the fourth time that Mr. Toft has won the Cup, first time in 1900, second in 1902, third in 1906. This is without doubt the most remarkable achievement of any competitor in the Exhibition. Chief Police Inspector Retires. We understand that Chief Inspector G. Phillips, of the Warrington Borough Police Force, has retired on pension. The resignation was tendered and accepted at the meeting of the Watch Committee on Thursday. Chief Inspector Phillips has been connected with the Warrington police force for the past eighteen years.

Music In the Park. The Borough Brass Band will play the following nrogramme of music in the Park on Sunday: Hymn, "Lead Kindly Light " ; march, "Ravenswood," W. Rimmer; overture, "Poet and Peasant," Suppe ; trom- bone solo, "In Native Worth," Haydn ; selection, "William Tell," Rossini; song, "Daddy Angel," V. emery; "Hallelujah Chorus," Handel; "God save the King." Conductor, Mr. T. Griffin.

The following directors and officials of the company attended: Messrs. A. C. Russell (chair- man), Richard T. Fairclough' J. Maginn, James Thompson, P. Magian (directors), F. Maginn (manag- ing director), and E. Fairclough (director and secretary). The annual balance sheet for the year ending 30th June was read and the following distri- bution of profits determined upon :—After providing for depreciation and for bad and doubtful debts, pay- ing directors' and auditors' fees, and adding £lOO to Ito the reserue, a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent., and a bonus of 21 per cent. was distributed to the ordinary, shareholders, .A. balance of 05 was also carried forward to next year's accounts. The com- pany's business continues to increase yearly, and to enable it to be dealt with advantageously recent additions to the capital and premises have been made. Mr. A. C. Russell, being the retiring director, was re-elected to the Board. Mr. J. R. Williams was re-elected auditor.

div.head: SHUNTING FATALITIES. Workmen Killed at Grosfield's and
div.p: SHUNTING FATALITIES. Workmen Killed at Grosfield's and
Monks, Hall's.

Two shunting fatalities were inquired into by Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, at the Warrington Police Station yesterday afternoon. The first case was that of John Lyons (20), 28, Gee-street, who was crushed between a waggon and a stop block at Messrs. Crosfleld's works, where he was employed as a labourer, on Thursday evening. Mr. A. iJewis, Chief Inspector of Factories for the district, watched the proceedings. NIL B. Evans, solicitor, represented Messrs. Crostield, and Mr. P. S. Steel appeared for the relatives. Fred Caldwell, sheeter, employed by the L. 45.: N.-W. Railway Co., stated that at 5.50 on Thursday evening he was washing his hands in a cabin on the premises of Messrs. Crosfield just before leaving off work for the day when he heard someone moaning. On looking through the cabin window he saw the deceased in a standing position wedged between a stop block and a waggon. He went to his assistance, but before he reached deceased, the waggon retreated from the stop block, allowing him to fall to the ground. Witness got him up and, with assistance, deceased walked to the works ambulance room. After being attended he was taken to the Infirmary where he died. In answer to the Coroner witness said he had never 'seen anyone leave the works by the Factory-lane gate. It was close to there that the accident occurred. The Coroner pointed out that there ware notices in the works which read: "Employees must not cross the lines usnecessarily. These sidings must be crossed only by the subway." Mr. Lewis said the arrangements at the works were such that if the work people would follow the orders and the notices and avail themselves of the subway, the danger which always attended shunting in the middle of a large works would be reduced to a minimum. He could not suggest anything further. The Coroner said that no doubt deceased was trying to get round by the last waggon and was squeezing himself between the buffers and the stop block when the engine pushed the waggons up and he was crushed. , A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned. Mr. Evans expressed the extreme regret of the firm at this unfortunate occurrence, and their deep sympathy with the relatives. The Coroner: Mr. St6el will see that you pay the proper amount in due time. (Laughter.) The death of Harry Massey (21). 30, Samuel-street, a shunter, who was killed at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. on Tuesday, was then inquired into. Mr. F. G. Taylor (Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co.) repre- sented the firm. - -

_ Charles Jones, engine driver employed by Monks Hall and Co., stated that on Tuesday afternoon he was engaged in shunting operations along with the deceased And was about to pick up an empty coat waggon. Deceased took the prop which was used for that purpose and having fixed it against the waggon gave witness the signal that all was right and the engine was started. The prop gave way when the engine touched It and swung ronnd striking the deceased who fell to the ground groaning. He was taken to the Infirmary where he died. . .

In answer to Mr. Lewis witness admitted that the waggon could have been moved by means of a pinch bar but that would have taked ten minutes or a quarter of an hour, whereas when the prop was used it took only about a minute. He had known the prop to slip before, but not often. Witness knew there was a regula- tion to the effect that the prop should not be used when other reasonably practicable means could be adopted. Mr. Lewis said the case afforded an object lesson in connection with the risks which were so often dis- cussed between managers of large concerns and him- self with regard to this practice. He hoped the firm would do what they could to reduce the risk by adopt- ing the pinch bar. Mr. Taylor promised that the stwgestion would receive the greatest consideration. The firm always thought propping was the only way of dealing with the work at that particular point and if Mr. Lewis could make any recommendation they would be pleased to adopt anything that was feasible. A verdict of, Accieental death" was returned.

div.head: PALACE THEATRE AND HIPPODROME
div.p: PALACE THEATRE AND HIPPODROME
fo be Opened on Monday Week.

On Monday week the new Palace Theatre and Hippodrome which has been erected at the junction of Barbanld-street and Friars' Gate will be opened to the public. The building has risen with wonderful rapidity and when an " Examiner " reporter visited it on Thursday a small army of workmen was engaged on the rich decorative work which, when completed, will make the interior sufficiently beautiful to please the most fastidious. Architecturally the theatre is an acquisition to the town and fully maintains the high reputation of Mr. r. G. Ward, architect, of Birmingham, who has been respon- sible for the erection of many successful theatres and music halls in the provinces. The builder is due of our own townsmen, Mr. C. W. Davenport, who is to be com- plimented upon the expeditious way in which the work has been carried out. The arrangements of the Palace , are on the most modern lines. One of the chief features is that an uninterrupted view of the stage can be obtained from all parts of the house. On the ground floor are arranged the pit stalls and pit, and on the first tier is a grand circle flanked on either side byhandsome canopied private boxes. There are also a spacious promenade and lounges, and on the second tier is a magnificent amphitheatre and gallery. The auditorium is capable of accommodating 2,000 persons, and it is being elaborately decorated with ornamental fibrous plaster, strikingly embellished in cream, terracotta and gold. The ceiling has .a domed centre from which will be suspended myriads of electric lights. The floor is paved with mosaic, whilst the walls and ceiling are beauti- fully decorated with ornamental plaster. Two handsome staircases lead from the hall to the grand circle. The theatre will be splendidly furnished and seated, and the stage arrangements are most complete. The dimensions are 60ft. by 30ft. and it is therefore capable of mount- ing almost any theatrical production travelling. 1 The utmost attention is paid to the safety and com- fort of visitors, the ventilation, heating, ftre-resistpg appliances and the means of ingress and egress being admirable—in fact it is claimed that there is nothing more up-to-date and complete in these respects in any 'other entertainment house in the world. Experts who have tested the acoustic properties of the theatre con- sider them unique. There will be two performances nightly, at 7 and 9 o'clock, and both entertainments will be identical. The leading London " stars" will appear in rotation, supported by novelties from the Continent and America. The house will be controlled and run under the personal supervision of Mr. Frank Macnaghten,who owns and operates the well-known variety theatres constituting the Macnaghten Vaudeville Circuit. Popular prices have been arranged and it is announced that the entertainment will at all times be found to please the family. Mr. Sydney Arthur will direct operations until the opening of the theatre and from that date the perma- nent resident manager will be Mr. G. D. Bradbury.

div.head: MESSRS. PEARSON & KNOWLES, LTD.
div.p: MESSRS. PEARSON & KNOWLES, LTD.
A Profitable Year.

' The thirty-fourth annual meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Ltd., will be held at , the offices of the Company in Bewsey-road, on Wednes- day, September 30th, when the report of the directors, and the balance sheet, will be presented. The report of the directors, Messrs. J. S. Harmood- Banner, M.P. (chairman), W. H. Bleckly, J. J. Bleckly, R. Brancker, W. Peter Rylands, and Herbert S. Bleckly, reads as follows : The profits for the year ending Jane 30th, 1907, amount to £110,680 3s. id., and the balance brought forward from last year is £9,323 7s. Bd., together £120,003 10s. 9d. An interim dividend at the rate of 6 per cent per annum on the preference shares and 5 per cent on the ordinary shares was paid in March last for the half- year ending December 31st, 1906, amounting to £22,375. The directors now recommend that a dividend be paid for the past half-year at the rate of 6 per cent per annum, on the preference shares and of 15 per cent per annum, free of income tax, on the ordinary shares, making with the interim dividend 10 per cent for the year,and a total distribution of £75,25t1. The Directors further recommend that £20,000 be added to the Reserve Fund, raising it to £150,000 ; that the sum of £15,755 14s. 10d., which represents the expenditure on capital account for the year, be written off, and that the balance of £8,997 15s. Ild, be carried , forward. The purchase of the shares of Rylands Brothers, Limited, mentioned in the Directors' Report in 1902, has now been completed, and the whole of the business transferred to this Company. The arrangements for the acquisition of shares referred to in the circular of March 28th last, giving to this Company the control of the Moss Hall and Wigan Junction Collieries have been completed, and the management has been transferred to this Company's officials. No profit from these investments is included in this year's account. _ ...•

The two operations referred to in thaiforegoing para- graphs have been financed by the issue of Bonds redeemable at two, three and five years. All departments of the Company's business show satisfactory results for the past year. In the iron and steel and engineering trades a good demand for home and foreign markets has kept the various branches of the works regularly employed at full production. The position of the coal trade up to the close of 1906 was disappointing, but has of late improved, and the out- look for the coming year is good. The Directors have to deplore the death of their late colleague Mr. George F. Pearson. In compliance with the Articles of Association, Mr. J. S. Harmood Banner, M.P., retires from the Board, and is eligible for re-election. The auditors, Messrs. Blease and Sons, also retire,and are eligible for re-election. The paid-up share capital of the company is £850,000, consisting of £250,000 Prefbrence and £610,000 Ordinary shares both £5 fully-paid, while, owing to the purchases referred to, there is now a further liability of loan capital, redeemable in two to five years, of £108,575. The present balance-sheet is the most satisfactory presented for many years past, and the following com- parison of the last three years' results will be of interest to our readers, as it is satisfactory to the share- holders of the company :- 1905. 1906. 1907. Net profit £57.196 £62,867 £110,680 Preference dividend
42,936 48,617 96,430 Ordinary dividend

-- Carried forward It will be seen that during the period under review there has been ,£30,440 spent out of revenue in exten- sions, while in the same time £40,000 has been similarly placed to reserve. This latter fund now amounts to £150,000, and a very satisfactory feature of the accounts is found in the investments against this of £191,140. The present report does not benefit from the acquisition of the Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Ltd., and the Moss Hall Wigan Junction Collieries, and in view of the statement that. the position of the coal trade was dis- appointing to the close of 1906, but that the outlook for the coming year is good, shareholders may, we think, naturally look for some return of prosperity which has recently been lacking. There is one very important feature in connection with this company ; the original valuation of the colliery leases and goodwill of collieries and ironworks was £315,(100, and the whole of this sum has been , written off out of profits, so that the present position of the company is of the healthiest character, and the recent advance in the shares is apparently fully justified.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The football season at Warrington opened with a flourish, for the locals showed fine form against Leigh and won by the largest score of the day, 28 points to 3. This is sufficient to be going on with, and proves that the Cup-holders are still in winning vein. The season following their first Cup victory saw them in rather poor form,but it is be to hoped that all the hard- won glory of last April will not depart this season,but instead be added to. There seems little chance of War- rington winning the Northern League yet awhile, but they might secure either the Lancashire Cup or the South Lancashire Cup just as an incentive to the struggle to hold again the Northern Union trophy.

There is plenty of youth and enthusiasm about the side, but one or two weaknesses need early attention. Chief among them is the right wing position, which was only moderately filled on Saturday by Dickenson, who is unsuited to the part. Brooks played half, and if he is going to remain there, another winger will have to be found somewhere. Jordan might train on, but a " flier " would be an acquisition, seeing the capable I centres the club possesses. Then, a little help among the forwards would be useful. The reserves are some- what uncultivated and on the light side, especially with Shugars and Preston among the abs?ntees. The first six cannot go through the season, and an effort should be made to stiffen the second string. Having pointed out these weaknesses we will proceed to distribute praise where merited.

The general fitness and smartness of the team com- manded admiration. They went off with a dash which brought five points in tw ) minutes,and generally out-classed the Leigh men from start to finish. In every department they were superior to the visitors, who seem a very ordinary lot and not likely to capture many trophies for the Leigh Football Club. It was somewhat of a surprise to find Leigh so weak, for a stiff game had been expected. They defended stubbornly, but on the attack were woefully weak and would never have crossed the Warrington line by their own unaided efforts. The try they got was more or less a present. There was practically only one failure on the home side, and as Dickenson is essentially a centre his want of scoring ability is excusable. The forwards were fast and strong, while the backs combined with a smartness which was both refreshing to see, and profitable to the team.l Altogether, Warrington made a very auspicious start to the 1907-8 season.

Fish had the honour of registering the first try of the season not only for Warrington but for the Northern Union. He was over the line in his own irresistible fashion a minute from the start on Satur- day, after as perfect a piece of half and three-quarter combination as one could wish to see. What a cheer there was from the 6,000 people sunning themselves round the rails! Isherwood early showed that his twelfth season is not going to be his worst, and he was the cleverest and mast resourceful centre on the field. Taylor also did well, and the halves, especially the dashing Brooks, were tip-top. It is still an open question whether Brooks is better at half or wing, but anywhere he is a first-class footballer. Tilley did splendidly at full-back, and seems to have a good season's play in him.

On the Leigh side there was very little talent noticeable. Young Higson gave a very creditable display at full back, and Tom Johnson was smart and speedy at centre, while the best of the forwards was the Warrington lad, Gallop. Paddy O'Neill seemed to get disgusted with the run of the tide against him, ' and did not shine as much as usual in the front rank of the pushers. The return of Molyneux and Clarkson should help the Leigh men considerably. Smith, the forward who scored 80 many tries on the wing last season, was no match for Fish, even though he did devote himself to shadowing the Warrington crack. " Jack " was noticeably in good trim, and I hope he is qualifying for the representative gimes against the All Blacks.

Warrington's match to-day is likely to prove a more severe trial than the one with Leigh. True,they generally win at Rochdale, but the Hornets ,have a better side this season than for some time past, and came very near to winning at Salford last week. The acquisition of the two Halifax threequarters, and Hartley,has strengthened the attack considerably, and Warrington will need to show their best form in order to secure the spoils.

Practically the same side as last week has been chosen, the only change being Preston for Belton. The substitution of Jordan for Dickenson might have been made with advantage for the former is certainly a more effective wing. The full side is : Tilley, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Taylor and Dickenson three- quarters; Lees and Brooks, half backs ; Boardman, Thomas, Heath, Harmer, Preston and Naylor forwards.

The "A" team opens at home to-day with the Hornets " A " as visitors, and a strong team has been chosen, viz. : Berry, fall back ; Landor, Cartwright, Jordan, and Kenyon threequatters ; Kaye •anrl Daintith, half-backs ; Belton, Jolley, Forster, P. Boardman, Bradshaw and Holbrook, forwards.

We are informed that a paragraph which appeared in this column on August 31st, with reference to Fish, gave offence to the popular three- quarter as the inference seems to have been drawn by some readers that Fish was serving a term of imprisonment for a criminal\ offence, which, of course, was not the case. We much regret that our jocular expressions should have been so interpreted,and tender to him our apology for any pain or annoyance we have unintentionally caused him.

By t e way, there is no definite news of the com- position of the New Zealand side as yet, though in our football column we publish the names of an unofficial selection which is said to be near the actual truth. Five of the best men among the original All Blacks are included, and altogether. the strength of the team seems unquestionable.

The final for the" Finlayson" Cup takes place to-day at Ban Quay, when Sankey Wire Mills will play Whitecross No. 1. The referee will be Mr. George Ball, jun. Gold medals as well as the cup will be pre- sented to the winners, whilst silver medals will be presented to the runners-up. If we have fine weather the games are sure to be most interesting.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

Warrington met South Hill at home on Thursday and registered a victory. In the first. half the visitors defended the deep end, and Warrington early attacked, C. Ashton scoring a grand goal. The same player added a second goal, and then Turner increased Warrington's lead. Pemberton added a fourth, and further goals were scored by C. Ashton and C. Turner,. Half-time— Warrington 6 goals, South Hill nil. In the second half the visitors forced the Ewe, and Woods saved smartly from Rennoson. A few mutes later Rennoson opened the score for South Hill. Sutton dribbled well and sent in a torrifie shot, which Foster saved well. Rennoson added a second goal for the visitors, and Haddon placed a third. Final—Warrington 6 goals, South Hill 3 goals.

div.head: BLIND MAN'S WONDERFUL FEAT.
div.p: BLIND MAN'S WONDERFUL FEAT.

- 7\ fr. 3. NV. Lawson, of Armley, Leeds, a blind piano ' tuner. took up cabinet-making as a hobby, and has actually made two inlaid mahogany tables, both of which have been purchased by the Queen of Roumania. Her Majesty takes a. deep interest in people afflicted by blindness, and is. In fact,forpaing a colony for the blind in Ilnkharest. She has invited Mr. Lawson to go to Roumania to teach the blind people cabiuet-making, and Mr. and Mrs. Lawson, who were only married last October, leave Leeds at the end of the month.

div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR. 'Edited by John Workman.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR. 'Edited by John Workman.

Readers of this column are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office, Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

I have received a copy of a new periodical. Under the title of "Spiders and Flies" it intends, from time to time, to expose advertising, commercial and financial frauds. The frauds, quacks or tricksters who will be exposed in the " Gazette " articles, says be writer, will include : Financial Frauds. Patent Medicine Frauds. Musical Instrument Frauds. Costume, Hat and Skirt Frauds. Electrical Care Frauds. Employment Frauds. Stage and Concert Frauds. Professional Hair Growers. ' Fortune-telling and Matrimonial Frauds. Auction Frauds. Photographic Frauds. I Turf Frauds. Fit Frauds. Deafness Frauds, etc. I wonder whether any good can come of such an exposure. The present competitive system lends itself so readily to fraud that the only lasting solution to the question can be found in a New Society. Business to-day is mostly rotten. it is creating a nasty smell. \ Contagion is inevitable. What are you going to do?

"Druakenness in Warrington" and doubtless the majority of your most intelligent readers will quickly recognise therein the same old, well-worn phrases and medieval, impracticable sentiments that have served as the general " stock-in-trade " (during the last twenty years) for a large number of the extremely superficial thinkers and re-actionary politicians so sadly prevalent amongst the teetotal advocates of this country._

Take for example the following quotation a rare old "chestnut" (Hats off—please.) "If the £167,000,000 spent annually on drink was turned into other industrial channels, unemployment would cease, and starvation would be for ever blotted out of the pages of our history."

Will Mr. Griffiths (or any of his teetotal colleagues) please mention the particular industrial channels, which with an additional annual turnover of ..f.,167,000,000 would permanently solve the unemployed and poverty problems? It is estimated that there are over 40,000,001) persons resident in the United Kingdom, which gives an average yearly drink expenditure of about £,4 per head or eighteen pence per week for every man. woman and child. Do our Good Templar friends seriously claim that an advance of three shillings to the wages of a married labouring man, at present in receipt of a miserable pittance of 18 shillings as " payment " for a full week's work, would actually lift that particular individual above the poverty Line? There are in this country thousands of really respect- able hard-working men and women who are total abstainers but who are still forced to exist in com- parative poverty and amidst almost joyless sur- roundings.

Perha—ps our teetotal friends may possibly be able, to account for the dire distess of the Irish peasants and the extreme destitution awl suffering of many millions of our fellow subjects in the Indian Empire amongst whom drunkenness is almost an unknown. evil.

The closing of every brewery, distillery, hotel, inn. and public-house in the land would inevitably result in a large displacement of labour directly affecting many thonsands of men and women. Would this additional .1:167,000,000 distributed into those "other industrial channel% " provide suitable work for all these persons, in addition to raising above the poverty line the millions living at present " on the verge of starvation," including an unemployed army of about 200,000?

JOHN WORKMAN. CHRISTIANITY AND SOCIALISM. THE CHRISTIAN SOCIALISTS. There is a portion of John Workman's last letter that calls for very plain speaking. This will not be withheld. I refer to that in which he quotes words of Frederick Denison Maurice, whom Charles Kingsley delighted to call " Master " to support his contention of the harmony between the Socialism he advocates and Christianity. The words quoted are these, "I seriously believe that Christianity is the only founda- tion of Socialism and that a true Socialism is the necessary result of a sound Christianity." John Workman knows very well (if he does not he ought to) that the Socialism of the noble band of men who were known as Christian Socialists, Maurice,Kingslev, Ludlow, Neale and Hughes, was something entirely, different from the Socialism he advocates. Maurice was at the head of this band, but Kingsley was its principal exponent. I could give many quotations from the writings of these men; one from Kingsley, will suffice. In writing to a friend on the work of the Christian Socialists he says : " We are teaching the working-men to become Christians by teaching them gradually that true Socialism, true liberty, brotherhood, and true I equality (not the carnal dead level equality of the Communist, but the spiritual equality of the Church ideas which gives every man an equal chance of developing and using God's gifts and rzwards every man accortling to his work without , respect of persons) is only to be found in loyalty I and obedience to Christ." I This is the " true Socialism" which both Kingsley and Maurice refer to. An equality before God, an equality of opportunity for development, rewarding every man according to his work! I humbly stand on the same platform with these good men. If they were Socialists —if this is Socialism—then I too am a Socialist. To reward every man according to his work is in accord with the teachings of Christianity. John Workman says "this is impracticable and unchristian." He will find this much easier to say than to prove. Maurice and Kingsley did not teach a single principle peculiar to modern Socialism, but opposed it with a virile force characteristic of the men. They taught that trust in State aid to reform individuals was foolish, that co-operation should be, voluntary,that instead of private cap:tal being robbery it was a divine stewardship, that men would never become true brothers by State plans. In so doing they struck at the very roots of the Socialism which John Workman now advocates. I am inclined to think that John Workman has found this quotation detached in some Socialist literature, and has never realised the import of the term " true Socialism "as used by Maurice. If this be so he has some excuse, but it indicates a carelessness that is scarcely pardonable in one who takes upon himself the editorship of a Socialistic column on a Liberal paper. Kingsley and Maurice are amongst my most valued library friends. Towards the former I have always felt a sort of a hero worship. To have the opinion of such friends used to support theories which I know they strongly opposed is not pleasant, and in loyalty to them I wish to clear their name from such associa- tion. I have too much respect for the noble band of Christian Socialists to allow their names to be used in support of a system fraught with grave danger to the common weal. I never came in direct contact with Kingsley, but I knew a good deal of his close friend "Tom "Hughes of "Tom Brown's Schooldays" fame. We have , together talked over these and many kindred matters, and I know of what I speak. One of my most treasured pictures is an excellent engraving of Charles Kingsley which I got through the kindness of Hughes. John Workman says that I misrepresent Socialism in the parable of the elder brother, and that Socialigts do not want to make all men equal in possessions. My reference to the right to equal shares arose out of the fact that the two men in question were brothers and therefore had a right to equal shares in the family inheritance. This reference to equality had nothing to do with Socialism, and therpfore was no misrepre- sentation. John Workman further says that "Mr. Parker emphasizes the notion that the kingdom of Heaven is something only in the next world, and that men are sent only to save what Kingsley called 'their own dirty souls.'" There is nothing in my letter to support this statement, and I wish John Workman would learn to be a little more accurate and not associate , words and ideas with my name that I have neither used nor conceived. John Workman accuses me of amiability. It certainly requires a good deal of amiability to conduct a correspondence with one who misrepresents your words in almost every p tragraph. John Workman does not seem to have grasped the distinction which I tried to make clear respecting regeneration coming from within as opposed to regeneration by compulsion from without. He instances the call to the disciples, and appears to consider it an instance of regeoeration from without. I may be at fault in the way I p‘ot the matter, but in this case, as in others, obedience to the Saviour's call sprang from within, was entirely voluntary. There was no compulsion; these men were free to refuse the call, indeed many did so. All through the teaching of Christ the free will of men is respected. If in any way Christ ritaae men do things it was only in the sense of a compulsion springing from love, and he ever left the upward initiative to arise from the free will of the individual. Men were urged as individuals to bear one another's hardens, to bear the infirmities of the weak, to love their neighbours as themselves. State Socialism would reverse all this as far as material things are concerned. Individual initiative would be sup- pressed, and the State become the universal alms- giver, the great burden bearer. The free moral action of the individual would be superseded, and this not by the consent of the whole but only with the approval of the majority. The area for the individual development of the Ohristian virtues would be narrowed and circumscribed and result in their ' enfeeblement. Officials would take the place of the On Thursday morning Mr. Charles Fuller Garland' of Samaritans. I strongly recommend Mr. Griffiths andloa followers to read carefully a few standard sociological works written by eminent modern authors, an'i I also venture to suggest that a perusal of the following books would be to them both profitable and instructive, and also interesting :—" The Life and Labour of the People of London," by Charles Booth; " Poverty," by Seerbohm Rowntree ; " Riches and Poverty," by Chiozza-Money, in addition 4to that encyclopredie masterpiece " The Temperance Problem and Social Reform "by Rowntree and Sherwell. In concluston, Sir, I believe that the Social Reformer having a genuine desire to effectively further the cause of true temperance must necessarily study systematically the complex social organism both iii its ethical and moral phases, but more particularly from an economic standpoint. To ridicule the proprietors of the brewing and allied industries and belabour with abusive insolence all our fellow men and women who are not strict teetotallers is not only illogical but extremely fallacious, and Mr. Griffiths and men of his ilk have, in the past, done incalculable harm to the temperance cause by their general attitude of intolerance and bigoted fanaticism. At least such is the candid opinion of

div.head: PRICE OF SOAP.
div.p: THE PRICE OF SOAP.
A Reduction under Competition.

A Birmingham correspondent writes :—Grocers and others in the Birmingham district were on Tuesday very much surprised at receiving a circular from Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, of Warrington, announcing a redaction of a half-penny per tablet in the price of their Perfection soap. This is the second important soap firm to announce a reduction. The alteration from 31d. to 3d. is said to follow upon similar action by Messrs. Watson and Sons in July, which, retailers state, is com- pelling other makers in self-defence to reduce prices. The drop is not to be explained by any change that has taken in raw material, which is said to be as dear as at the time of the combine. Messrs. Crosfield's circular notifies a reduction "to exactly the same wholesale basis ruling previous to Pehruck,l, 1. 'Miln. rcAtitAluu will enable you to vire the public the immediate benefit of a return to the threepenny retail figure. We shall he glad to give you the credit of a ss. per gross rebate on any stock in your warehouse from date." Messrs. !Knight and Co., of London, shave also reduced their brand one halfpenny, Messrs. Gossages have increased the weight of their tablets, like Lever Brothers.

MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S ATrIDIIDE. In an interview at Warrington, on Wednesday, one of the directors of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons said the firm had simply been forced by competition to make the reduction, which could not be said to be justified by any lowering in the cost of production. The slight fall in raw material would not be a sufficient reason in itself, and certainly nothing one could call a distinct break of prices had occurred. The present reduction must mean for the moment considerable sacrifices on the part of manufacturers, and could not be maintained indefinitely unless the market for raw materials came to their relief. The reduction was brought about entirely by the exigencies of competition, and was merely following upon the action taken by another firm.

div.head: " REDUCTION UNJUSTIFIABLE."
div.p: " REDUCTION UNJUSTIFIABLE."

The managing director of John Knight, Ltd ~ explained the reason for therr reduction in the pride of soap to a Press representative on Monday. "The reduction," he said, "is quite unjustifiable. It is due solely to under-cutting competition, and we and other firms have reduced our prices simply because we have been compelled to do so. We have no desire to make a reduction, and we are doing it at a loss. There is nothing to justify it. flaw materials are just as dear to-day as they were in February last, when prices went up so high that manufacturers had to put a halfpenny on the retail mice of their soap. But we cannot help, ourselves. Messrs. Crosfield have reduced the price,and if we want to keep our customers there is no course open to us but to follow the ' lead. It is all due to Messrs. Crosfield treading on the toes of other manu- facturers."

Soapmakers assert that the public have never taken to the 3kl. tablet. Having got into the habit of paying 3d. per tablet for their soap, they would not pay more, even though the tablet might weigh a full pound. The result was that certain manufacturers produced a 3d.. tablet, and this was taken up by the public to such an extent that other manufacturers, in order to protect themselves, had to put on the market a tablet to be sold retail at 3d. The first to do this was Messrs. Watson, and now other manufacturers are bound to follow suit, either by reducing the price or increasing the weight.

div.head: MESSRS. GOSSAGE'S ACT/ON.

Our prices and weights have been arranged so as to leave practically the same profit aa was obtainable on the sizes introauoed after the advance of 4s. per hundredweight in February last."

div.p: FAIRY TALE, FROM THE GERMAN.

o.The Holiday Postcard Competition is now closed, and I am very pleased indeed with the large number of postcards sent me. I am going through these very carefully, and I hope to announce the winners next week.

I mentioned that I wanted a special effort made to secure more members for our Corner. I do not only require members, but I want more short stories and anecdotes from my Nieces and Nephews. The best way to increase our mem- bership is to ask all of you to do your utmost during the next two months. To the one send- ing me the greatest number of names and addresses of those wishing to join I shall send a beautiful casket of Fry's Chocolate.; other prizes will also be awarded. Now, please, all of you, do your best to persuade your young friends to join our League. Nearly every week I am giving away dainty little pocket mirrors for stories, etc. With love until next week, UNCLE NZD.
In those olden times when wishes were yet of some avail, there lived a king whose youngest daughter was so surpassingly beautiful that even the sun himself was surprised when he shone on her face. •

A great gloomy wood grew near this king's castle, and in the wood, under an old linden tree, there was a well. When the weather was hot, and the young princess felt weary of the castle walls, she would run to the shady wood, and, seated on the brink of the cool well, play with her golden ball—she knew no pleasanter pastime than to throw it high into the blue air, and catch it as it fell back again to the earth. It happened that once, as she,was amusing herself in this manner, the golden ball slipped from her little hand, and rolled into the well. The princess watched it sink; lower and lower it went, until at last she could see it no more. Then she wept bitterly, and it seemed as if she could not be comforted, when suddenly she heard a voice, which said, "Why dost thou mourn so, 0 king's daughter? Thy tears would move a stone to pity I" The princess looked in the direction of the sound, and perceived a frog stretching his ugly little head out of the water. "Oh, it is thou; old water-splasher!" cried she; "I am weeping for my pretty ball, which has fallen in the well."

"Cry no more, then," answered the frog; "I can help thee; but what wilt thou give me if I restore thy plaything?" "Whatever thou wishest, dear frog!" replied the maiden; "my clothes, my jewels, and even the golden crown I wear!" "Thy clothes, thy jewels, and thy golden crown I care not for," said the frog; "but, if thou will promise to love me, to make me thy companion and playfellow, to let me sit near thee at thy little table, eat from thy little golden plate, drink from thy little golden cup, and sleep in thy little bed, then will I go down into the well, and fetch up thy ball." " I will promise thee all," cried the princess; "whatever thou wilt, only bring me My ball again 1" (To be continued.)

div.head: TOO -SLOW.
div.p: TOO -SLOW.

In a Lancashire town, an Inspector visited a mill to see that the owners did not employ chil- dren under a certain age. The manager tele- phoned through the mill, and all the little ones who were wrongfully employed were hidden ,in various out-of-the-way places. Whilst crossing the yard, the Inspector happened to observe some fingers protruding from a case, and, on lifting the lid, he saw a small boy sitting down. He asked him why he was there, upon which the little fellow replied: "Shut th' mouth, mon, and put t' lid down. Doesn't ta know th' In- spector's about ?" MARJORIE SCOTT.

div.head: SURPRISE.
div.p: A SURPRISE.

There were two Irishmen, named Pat and Mike, once engaged to clean some very high windows. They could not think of a way to get at them for some time. Then they thought they would get a ladder, and put it through the win- dow, and Mike sit inside, and Pat outside. When they had got nicely started, Mike sud- denly remembered that he had left some of his rags behind him. Calling to Pat to stay there a minute or two, as he was going down he ran downstairs to fetch them. Arriving in the street, to his great surprise, he found Pat sitting in the middle of the street, rubbing his legs and shins. "Why, Pat," he exclaimed, "you are down first; which way did you get?" J. CUMMINS.
A FIJIAN DANCE.

The Fijians are, perhaps, the best dancers in the world. One of the most curious dances that they practise is one representing a tide rising on a reef. The idea to be conveyed, Miss Gor- don Cumming tells us in her recent book on Fiji, is that of a tide gradually rising on a reef, till at length there remains only a little coral isle, round which the angry breakers rage, flinging their white foam on every side. At first the dancers form in long lines and approach silently, to represent the quiet advance of the waves. After a while the waves break up into smaller companies, which advance with out- spread hands, and bodies bent forward to repre- sent rippling wavelets, the tiniest waves being represented by children. Quicker and quicker they come on, now advancing, now retreating, yet, like true waves, steadily progressing and gradually closing on every side of the imaginary islet round which they play or battle after the manner of breakers, springing high in mid-air and flinging their arms far above their heads to represent the action of spray. As they leap and toss their heads, the soft white masi or native cloth—which, for greater effect, they wear as a turban with long streamers, and also wear round the waist, whence it floats in long scarf-like ends—trembles and flutters in the breeze. The whole effect is most artistic, and the orchestra do their part by imitating the roar of the surf on the reef—a sound which to them has been a never-ceasing lullaby from the hour of their birth..

div.head: CARLO AND NAN.
div.p: CARLO AND NAN.

Carlo is a great, black, splendid dog. Nam is a little, white, naughty kitten—such a naughty, thievish kitten! "She must be put out of the way," said mamma. "I can't have her into things so." "Very well," said papa; "I'll send Peter up to see to it." "Oh, no, no 1" cried Trotty; "please ddn't send Peter to see to it. You see, Nan belongs to Trotty." "Yes," said mamma; "the very next time she's caught steal- ing she'll have to be taken care of." , Trotty knew what that meant, and he began to cry. Carlo thumped his black tail hard upon the floor and growled a little. He didn't like to hear Trotty cry. Maybe he didn't want an taken care of just in that way, either. But the next time Nan 70 6 caught stealing, it was Carlo who caught her. Nan jumped up on the table and began to lap cream out of a bowl. Carlo growled and showed his teeth. Nan jumped down again in a great hurry. Carlo took her in his mouth and shook her, and dropped her beside the stove. Then he trotted out to his kennel, and pretty soon he came back with a chicken bone. He laid that down before Nan with a little purring growl. "There," said he, "eat that and don't steal any more cream. If you do—" At least that is what mamma, who was watching, told Trotty that Carlo said; and phe had to tell the story more times than half-a- dozen. And nobody has caught Nan in a theft since that day, unless it is Carlo; and Carlo never'll tell—so Trotty says.

There was quite a row at a recent meeting in a Richmond, U.S.' chapel-vestry between Uncle Mose and Deacon Gabe Snodgrass. "You is the biggest black rascal in Austin," said Deacon Snodgrass. "You is a heap bigger one," re- turned Mose, placing his hand on the ivory handle of his umbrella. " Bredderen," inter- posed Parson Blodsoe, "you talks as if dar was nobody else present 'ceptin' yerselfs."

div.head: TO MAKE A HAPPY HOME.
div.p: TO MAKE A HAPPY HOME.

1. Learn to govern yourselves, and to be gentle and patient. 2. Guard your tempers, especially in seasons of ill-health, irritation, and trouble, and soften them by prayer, penitence, and a sense of your own shortcomings and errors. 3. Never speak or act until you have prayed over your words or acts, and concluded that Christ would have done so in your place. _
4. RemeMber that, valuable its is the gift of speech, the gift of silence is often much more valuable.

5. Do not expect too much from others, but remember that all have an evil nature, whose develoPment we must expect, and which we should forbear and forgive, as we often desire forbearance and forgiveness ourselves. 6. Never retort a sharp or angry word. It is the second word that makes the quarrel. 7. Beware of the first disagreement. 8. Learn to speak in a gentle tone of voice.
9. Learn to say kind- and pleasant things whenever an opportunity offers.
10. Study the character of each, and sym- pathise with all in their troubles, however small.
11. Do not neglect litge things, if they can affect the comfort of others in the smallest degree. 12. Avoid moods and pets and fits of -sulki- ness.
13. Learn to deny yourself, and to prefer others.
14. Beware of meddlers and tale-bearers. 15.. Never charge a bad motive if a good one is conceivable.
SCARED.

We remember the story of a woman who woke one night and found the house on fire—or be- ginning to burn—and who did not rouse the family or say a word, but bravely put out the fire, went to bed again, and no one else knew what had happened till morning. It is curious to see the difference in people when danger threatens. Some 'fly to pieces" as soon as any alarm comes, and do all they can to exaggerate a small scare into a big one—and these are not always women either. The "Denver Weekly News" tells how a scared negro servant roused the people in every room of a large boarding- house in that city by his fright. He slept in the basement.. At about eleven o'clock on the night in question, while peacefully snoring upon his humble cot, he heard suspicious noises out doors. Instantly the thought that the house was being in danger of broken into by robbers flashed through his massive brain, and he leaped to his feet, and, seizing a pistol, proceeded to fire away rapidly and in- discriminately, not caring where the, bullets went, so long as they had the effect a Lighten- ing away the burglars without harming him. They had the effect of scaring every one else in the house out of all scientific calculation, and of arousing the neighbours for a stone's-throw in all directions, and bringing them upon the streets in costumes not at all suited to an after- noon saunter along Larimer-street- And it was all causc_d by a poor, innocent cow, who was trying to extricate her foot from an empty paint- pot into which she had thrust it.
"Well," said an old gentleman who stumbled as he was trying to make his way around a group of waltzers, "this is really working one's passage round the whirled."
They must have learned sheep in Texas, for a farmer in Travis advertises for "an industrious man, to take general charge of five thousand sheep, who can talk Spanish."

Rev. Dr. Tyng, of New York, when a theo- logical student, officiated at a church in a neighbouring town, and, on his way to preach one morning, met an aged coloured man. "Well, uncle, do you ever go to hear the young preacher I" asked the unfledged doctor. "Nor massa," replied the negro; " dis chile don't let. none a' dem students practise on him."

Would Rather be Shot. Frank Millington, butcher, Stockton Heath, was charged at Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, with stealing a fowl, valued at 2s. 6d., the property of Henry Miller, of Stretton.—Sergeaut Barlow said he met prisoner in Old London-road on Sunday evening and stopped him.. Underneath his coat was a butcher's apron in which the fowl produced was wrapped. The fowl was quite warm, and did not appear to have been dead an hour. There was blood about its head. • Witness locked prisoner up, and on Monday charged him with stealing the fowl. In reply prisoner said he found the fowl on some refuse on Mr. Miller's premises, and was taking It away for the purpose of getting maggots.-- Defendant protested that be had not stolen the fowl, and said he would rather the Bench shoot him than his character should be disgraced.--Defendant was fined Xkl and costs (.£2 6s. altogether) or 14 days' imprisonment. • , Scene In aW arks:

John Lomas, 54, Donee-row, Cockhedge, Warring- ton, was summoned at Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, for assaulting Thomas Gerrard on August 3rd, Complainant -vPho is a watchman at the Latch- ford Tube Works, said defendant came to his work over a hour late and he(complainant) told him he was not fit for his position that night and advised him to go home —Defendent struck complainant a violent blow in the throat, kicked him over the left leg and tried to trip him. He also struck complainant in the eye, cansing a cut. Frank Hinton, fireman at the Tube Works, gave evidence in support of complain- ant's 3380 —Defendant said no one was in the lodge when he arrived at the w.,rks.and he walked through a door. He did not speak to the watchman (complain- ant) until he said defendant was incapable. Defend- ant made an attempt to go to his work; but com- plainant pushed him. Defendant then lost his temper and struck complainant. —The Bench said an assault had been committed, and defendant would be fined S,l and costs.

GARDEN TENTS.—Tennis, Croquet, and other out- door sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Cage Bird Society. The annual meeting of the Penketh, Sankey and District Garden and Cage Bird Society was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, on Monday evening. The prizes awarded at, the last exhibition (which was held on August 17th),were distributed. Several items of interest were discussed and the following committee was elected for the ensuing Year, viz. : Messrs. J. Ditchfield, W. Woods, S. Andrews, It. Long, E. Houghton, E. Foster, J. Knowles, T. Bell, H. Mainley, Faulkner. IV. Moores, J.. Backhouse ' • also vice- presidents, Mrs. J. B. Aitken, Miss Bolton, Mrs. Chadwick, Mrs. Garnett, Mrs. Houghton, Miss Tinsly Miss M. Tinsly, the Rev. J. R. Jones and Messrs. .1. B. Aitken, C. Caird, James Dodds., John Dodds, R. ,Jenks, E. A. Murphy, C. E. Parker, J. F. Smitl). W. Walker, J. Waiters, P. Garnett, J. T. Ambler, D. Aldcroft ; Treasurer, Mr. H. Hope. The society has made rapid progress of; Lte years. ' ,The report and balance sheet, as read by the Secretary, were passed, and it is pleasing to note that the society has a balance in hand of Gs. 31-d. •In the report Of the secretary, a special wish was expressed- to the inhabitants of the district " that/they should take a deeper interest in the working of the society and so make the exhibition second to none around the district." Independent Labour Party.

Councillor Stott was the speaker at the open-air meeting in connection with the Independent Labour Party, held at Bridge Foot on Sunday evening. Mr. E. Horrocks presidA. Councillor Stott devoted a large R)rtion of his address to dealing with Lord Stanley's favourite phrase "Blackmailers and Bloodsuckers," which was used during the agitation of the postmen for better conditions. The ccmcessi^ns asked for by the postmen could be granted for one and a quarter The profit made by the postal service in 1904 was nearly four fnillions, Councillor Stott dealt with the history of the Stanley's, and said they owned 63,867 acres with an annual rent of at least half a million. The speaker gave instances of the prices which the public had had to pay to the Stanley's for land which was required for improvements. He then dealt with the Old Age Pension question continuing that when men of high rank received handsome pensions from the Government, the workers were alto entitled to them. The total income in this country amounted to £1,700.000,000. One and a qui.rter million people got 585 millions 31 million got 245 millions, 38 million got 880 millions. Half of the wealth was taken by one ninth of the population. One third of the income was.taken ty less than one thirtieth of the population 710,000 difd each year. 685,000 were worth 30 millions, and 25,000 were worth P5O millions. On Monday evening -Mr. J Hampson deliveted an interesting address. There was a large attendance.

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT. THE REVISING —BARRISTER AND PARTY COMPROMISES The Value of the Vote.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT. THE REVISING —BARRISTER AND PARTY COMPROMISES The Value of the Vote.

--- Mr. C. H. M.Wharton,who has succeeded the late Mr. J. T. Foard as revising barrister, held his first Court at Warrington on Monday morning. Very little public interest was taken in the proceedings* the business being exceptionally light. Seventy-nine claims and forty-nine objections were down for decision. Mr. J. Howes, jun., represented the Liberal party and Mr. W. Holbrook appeared for the 'Conservatives. Amongst others present were :—Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. W. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer), Mr. E. C. Cooper (assistant overseer for Winwick), Mr. J. Smith. (assistant overseer for Great Sankey), Mr. T. J. Garnett and Mr. E. H.•Ankland(relieving officers.) REVISING BARRISTER WELCOMED. Mr. W. Holbrook said be had great pleasure in welcoming his Honour on the occasion of his first Revision Court at Warrington. It was many years since they had seen a new face at the Court, and he hoped big Honour would be as successful as his prede- cessor, the late Mr. Foard, whose sudden death gave them great sorrow. Mr. Howes endorsed the remarks of Mr. Holbrook. He could assure the revising banister that anything the two party agints could do to render his duties light and pleasant would always be done. He thought his Honour would find that Warrington was one of the best places he would have to visit. The Revising Barrister said he thanked them for their kind remarks. lie could only say that the position of everyone who bad to discharge the functions of a judicial office was always made easier by the kindness of those who had to appear at the Court. He was told that everything had gone on smoothly in Warrington up to now and be felt certain they would continue to do so.

A LODGER CLAIM. Peter Lamb Edgar, 127, Winwick-road, applied for a lodger vote. Mr. Howes said he would like his Honour's ruling on the question of lodger votes as different barristers held different views. The Revising Barrister : This is apparently a case of father and son. _ _
Mr. Holbrook said that was so. The Revising Barrister (t,, claimant) : Haveyou got an arrangement with your father to occupy rooms as tenant?
Claimant.: Yes, eir. Mr. Holbrook: I think it is a zond claim in every way. He has the sole use of a bedroom and sitting- room. The Revising Barrister: Is no one also allowed to use them? _

Claimant: No, sir. Mr. Howes asked his Honour whethes he held that sons living with their parents were bona. fide lodgers? The Revising Barrister : That has been held, as long as they pay. Claimant gave evidence that he told for the rooms and produced a certificate to that effect. The Revising Barrister said he could not go behind the decision which said that if a son paid his father so mach for the exclusive use of a room and that sum was sufficient value, the vote. must be allowed. The only question was as to what extent he believed the •claimant's story. He could see no reason to doubt it, and therefore allowed the vote. FRIVOLOUS OBJECTIONS CONDEMNED. During the hearing of another case the Revising Barrister said he was strongly of opinion that objections ought not to he made unless there was some substance on which to base them. The rest of the business of the sitting was of a formal character.

EVFNING SITTING. "SOLE SUPPORT" Another sitting of the Court was held on Monday -evening. In a casa in which a vlte was claimed by the Con- servatives, Mr. 1-Tolbrook said the son was the sole -support of the mother, and she wished him to have the vote. In former Courts the Barrister bad granted such The moth.r stated that she was still the tenant. The Revising Barrister: Then I cannot allow the claim. Mr. Holbrook: It was a ruling of the late Mr. Foard that when the son was the support of the mother he should have the vote. In this case the mother could not keep the house open withont the son's help and the house is not sufficiently qualified for the man to have a lodger vote. The Revising Barrister : All she has to do is to transfer the tenancy to the son. I cannot allow the -vote.

SPONTANEOUS HEATING OF HAY. In • a publication entitled Die Selbster- hitzung des .Heus, Hugo Miche gives an ac- count of some interesting experiments on the spontaneous heating of hay. These re- searches shew that, as had long been sup- posed, this is due to bacteriological„ action. Miche has isolated and cultivated the various micro-organisms which either directly or in- directly take part in the process. An account of the behaviour of each species under cul- ture is given. Besides those causing the change a number of fungi and bacteria which find their natural habitat in the heated hay have been isolated. Some of the species are pathogenic, and the fact that these seem to have their natural habitat in heated plant re- mains" is new. The highest temperature ob- served in a heating stack was 155 deg. Fahr. At a certain stage it was. found that self- sterilisation occurred, and the organisms all died off.

div.head: FUNGI IN HEATED RICKS.
div.p: FUNGI IN HEATED RICKS.

- - - Mr. J. Adams, writing on the same subject in the Irish Naturalist, draws attention to the high temperatures at which fungi can grow. He found fungi growing in the centre of heated ricks in which the thermometer rose to 135}deg. Fahr. THE SOAPBERRY TREE. The soapberry tree, Sapindus marginatua ntilis, has been quite extensively cultivated in Algeria for its berries, which are rich in saponin, and are, sent to Germany for use in the manufacture of soap. . Similar quali• ties are possessed by the Florida soap tree. Sapindus manatensis utilis, commonly known as the China soap tree, from the fad that it was originally introduced from China. Mr. E. Moulie, of Jacksonville, Fla., has been engaged in promoting the cultivation of this tree in the Southern States by a free distribution of seeds. The tree grows to 8 height of. 401 t. or 50ft., and begins to beas fruit in the sixth year. The berries are about the size of ober fieo, and consist of a hara, yellow-brown wax-like shell, enclos• big a large black seed. The shell is rich in sapenin, and if bits of it are agitated in water a lather will at once begin to ferm. By grinding the shells a brownish soap pow- der is obtained, - which • possesses valuable cleansing properties. The hard, black seeds of the soapberry tree have . been used in the manufacture of beads; they also yield a fine oil useful in soap manufacture, as well as in other industries.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. R. PTERPOINT.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. R. PTERPOINT.

The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. R. Pierpoint regretting his inability to be present he having to be in London on Wednesday in order to accompany his wife to a wedding at Canterbury. This was an appotnt- ment, of long standing.

div.head: ADDRESS BY THE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ADDRESS BY THE CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN (Councillor Fulton-Smith) said it gave him great pleasure to preside over that interesting gathering. He was struck with the title of their lodge —the word "loyal."He thought that when men were loyal to each other, there was every hope not only for them- selves but to those association with them. (Hear, hear.) That sort of Society had been in existence for many years. Its origin dated as far back as to the days of King Solomon. In those days communication with distant parts was difficult, and a plan was hit upon whereby the, genuine workman could be recognized when be landed on strange shores, and they adopted a system of symbols and signs. Those symbols and signs soon spread among artificers of different grades, so that when a workman passed from one country to another and he was challenged be was able to give the sign, and that was a guarantee he was an honest man and a man who could be taken in and be entertained. That Society encouraged thrift, they all knew that the back bone of England had been the thrift of its inhabi- tmte. Tne Illtlre that idea was followed the hatter for this country instead of depending non the visionary idea of old-age pensions which had no foundation what- ever. They were doing the best thing for old-age pensions by building up a society of that kind and it could be broadened out so that there would be a true spirit of independence because one would feel he had added his contributions to the general store of funds and was thereby entitled to receive the best benefit which the Society could confer upon him. It was with that view he would like to draw their attention to the vagaries which had been promulgated at the Trades Union Congress. Some of the leaders who told them that every man and woman was to have a pension, but not one of them attempted to show the method whereby the pension was to be secured but how was the money to be got. It was such a wide question that it would take years before it thoroughly developed itself in the minds of the community. It was all very well to say there were lots of people who would not take advan- tage of a pension fund, but he would like to say that if a pension scheme were ever adopted in this country it should be compulsory to -every man and woman to take advantage of it so that there would be no mistake as regarded the averages which was the basis of calculation and no one would be overlooked and no one would feel he was singled out as being the recipient of what some people called pauperism. There was plenty of ability among the workmen of this country to think out those things for themselves, and not trnst to some vagary who had perhaps never been in a friendly society and 'who wanted to get all he could out of his neighbour. Self help had always been recognized as the best help of all, and the man who helped himself was not behind in helping others. He believed one of the main problems of their society was based upon care, industry prudence and foresight. One feature of the society which struck hid very much was that they did not con- fine their borders to England. They were as wide as the British Empire. That was a splendid idea, for they were encouraging others in foreign lands to follow the same noble principles they followed in this country, which he believed to be the best for every man to follow based on the best of all books, the Bible. (Applause.) SIR GILBERT GREENALL,PRESENTS THE PRIZES:

Sir GILBERT GREEN.A.LL, in presenting the prizes said he thought the people of Warrington knew that he was always anxious to do anything be could to promote the sports and games in this country. (Hear, hear.) He felt that those sports, as they knew them in good old England brought out what was best in a man, both physical .ind moral. He could thoroughly congratulate the winners upon their success, and he hoped it would not be the last time they would ask him to give away the prizes. (Applause.) Captain PQTTER proposed a vote of thanks to Sir Githert for his presence, and for giving the cup, and observed that all of them greatly appreciated his generosity. He (Captain Potter) wished they had more support from the gentry of the district who would say, like Sir Gilbert, " If you will help yourselves we will help you." Bro. J. PARR seconded, and Sir Gilbert's health was drunk with musical honours. .

_ Sir GILBERT GREENALL in reply wild he bad thoroughly enjoyed the "smoker," and congratulated them upon its success. The donors of the prizes were thanked on the motion of Bro. DUCKWORTH, seconded by Bro. BAsturivrt,LE, and Mr. S. N. GREEN replied. k vote of thanks was passed to the artistes—the Warrington Harmonic Glee party, snd Messrs. G. Ratcliffe, H. Carter, Hughes,Winstanley, and E. Walker and Messrs. J. Forster and F. Wolfenden (accompanist) —on the proposition of Bro. Adams, seconded by Bro. J. Ashton. The CHAIRMAN was thanked for presiding on the proposition of Bro. L. Weir, who referred to Coun- cillor Fulton-Smith's kindness in presenting a gold medal, seconded by Bro. Holford. At the close, Bro. Edgar announced, amidst applause, that Councillor Fulton-Smith had consented to become an honorary member of the Warrington District.
