div.head: "A Message of Hope for the Drunkard."
div.p: "A Message of Hope for the Drunkard."

Sir,—May 1 call the attention of your readers— especially Magistrates—to the Special Clauses in the Government Bill of Probation for Offenders, which has now received Royal Assent, aod which gives Magistrates a splendid opportunity of reforming offenders brought before them for drunkenness and petty offences due thereto. Magistrates now have the power to say to an offender that, to obtain the merciful consideration of the Court, he may purge his offence and avoid the stain and ignominy of a conviction, provided he will promise not to drink for a prescribed period. Failure to keep such promise renders him liable to be arrested, convicted and punished for his original offence. This is practically the Man which Judge Pollard initiated in his Court at St. Louis, and by which, after a four years' trial, he has saved hundreds of drunkards; 98 per cent, keeping the pledge. May I appeal to Magistrates and Social Reformers everywhere to use the opportunity now given them to save drunkards from themselves and for their families. Enforce the pledge, and thereby reduce the vast army of 500,000 drunkards who are convicted every year in the Police Courts of this Christian country. I shall be happy to send full particulars and Pledge Forms on receipt of stamped reply envelope.—Yours faithfully,
WALTER EAST, Hon. Sec. The National Independent Temperance Party.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Convict's Daughter."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Convict's Daughter."

Stories which touch upon convict life are always popular with the multitude and a powerful melodrama with the title "The Convict's Daughter" has attracted large audiences to the Royal Court Theatre this week. The play teems with thrilling incidents, the most notable being the escape of the convict from the gloomy prison by means of a passing train. The scene is wonderfully well contrived and, as may be imagined, there is great excitement when the prisoner eludes the guard, leaps on to a railway waggon and, and although rifles are levelled at him, manages to get away unhurt. Of course, the convict is the hero of the piece for he has been wrongfully imprisoned, but in the end his character is cleared and retribution falls in the proper quarter. The prisoner has an attractive daughter whose chequered fortunes are second only in interest to her father's, and the play never becomes dull but entertains throughout. Mr. Frank Bertram earns chief honours as Michael Grahame—a part which he has played over 2,000 times. He is a most versatile actor,for while greatly amusing the assembly, in the intoductory stages as Weary Willie,the philoso- phical tramp, he rises to fine dramatic heights when, re-captured, he once more becomes" convict 89." His "make-up "is particularly effective. Mr. Bertram is supported by a capable company, Miss Lilias Deane giving a very pleasing portrayal of "The Convict's daughter." Mr. Escot Robson has a very unpopular part as Jaspar Thorn, the unscrupulous nephew, but he does full justice to it,the villainy being so realistic as to occasionally arouse the resentment of the more demonstrative section of the audience.

div.head: Next Week's Programme.
div.p: Next Week's Programme.

Next week Mr. Samuel James will present the famous drama "Saved from the Sea" by Arthur Shirley and Ben Landeck, as played at the Princess's Theatre;London. The play is a most interesting one, one of the chief incidents being an explosion at sea, followed by an exciting rescue. Mr. David G. Noble will appear in the leading part of Dan Ellington, a haaidy fisherman. which he has played with conspic- uous success, and Miss Marie Auckland will figure as Nancy Ellington, Dan's wife. The play will be splendidly mounted and should prove a great attrac- tion.

div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
div.p: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
Committee Meeting. Letter from New Zealand Secretary.

A- Rugby Union was held at the George Hotel, Hudders- field, on Tuesday evening, Mr. H. Ashton (Warrington) presiding. It was decided that the International match England v. Wales be played on Easter Monday. The following letter was read by Mr. J. Platt, the Secretary of the Union New Zealand Rugby Football Club, Kelbarne Parade, Wellington, N.Z., 22nd August, 1907. To the Secretary, Northern Football Union.—Dear Sir. We have com- pleted arrangements to play three matches in Sydney, N.S.W.,on the 17th, 21st,and 24th August with the newly formed professional team there. This necessitates us changing our route, and travelling via Sydney and Suez. I cabled saying we were leaving New Zealand on the 17th inst., but we shall now leave a week earlier so as to arrive in time for the sth October match with 7011. Now that New Zealand players see that the tour is assured they are all anxious to come, and are applying /or places every day. The majority of them are good men too. I have promised them that if we have a suc- cessful season this time I will organise a tour some subsequent season, and give them all consideration when making the final selection. I will bring some correspondence that will give you an idea how amateurs regard our present tour. I have, etc., A. H. BASKERVILLE.

Accompanying the letter was a newspaper cutting referring to a debate which had taken place at the Petone Junior Club Rooms, in the Wellington district, on the Question " Is professionalism in any form desir- able in New Zealand Rugby football ?" After a long debate an almost unanimous vote was declared in favour of professionalism. THE TOURISTS FR OM NEW ZEALAND.

div.head: PROBABLE CONSTITUTION OF THE SIDE.
div.p: PROBABLE CONSTITUTION OF THE SIDE.

Although the official list of the names of the twenty-five New Zealand footballers, who are on their way to nuke a professional tour in the North of England. has not yet been supplied to the Northern Tinton authorities, an nnofficial list of twenty-one "probable starters "arrived by the Australian mail on Tuesday. The names contained in the list are : McGregor, Pearce, Turtill (Canterbury), Smith, Wynyard, Todd, W. Tyler, Cunningham, Francis, and Gillett (Auckland), Eckhold, Johnstone (Otago), Tyne, Cross, Wright. Byrne, Kelly, Baskerville, Watkins (Wellington), Wrigley (Wairarapa), Colman (Taranaki). It is believed that one or two of the players named were not in the party that sailed from Sidney on August 24th, but the list may be taken as a fair indica- tion of the strength of the side. Five of the players now Railing for England on the Ortona were in the famous "All Blacks" team, viz.: Duncan McGregor and G. W Smith (three-quarters),G. Gillet, W.Cunningham, and W. Johnstone (forwards). Some of the other players are of international class, Cross, formerly of Petrone, is regarded as one of the foremost scrummagers in New Zealand, and one who distinguished himself against Bedell-Sivewright's team, which toured New Zealand some years ago. Tyne is a prominent South Island forward, and the Baskerville menteoned is the brother of the manager of the team.

div.head: IN A MUSICIAN'S HOME.
div.p: IN A MUSICIAN'S HOME.

William M. Hutchinson is well-known as the composer of" Dream Faces," " Ehren on the Rhine" and many other charming ballads. In his Isle of Wight home he keeps a Columbia Graphophone for his own pleasure and to entertain his friends and guests. The Columbia Phopograph Company had a letter from him in which he mentioned that a score of young people were coming in to an impromptu dance and he was going to play dance music on the Graphophone, "which will, I think, go better than a man at the piano and save 215." That illustrates only one advantage of having a Columbia Graphophme. That these instruments are built to last a lifetime is the conviction of all who use the Columbia kind. A customer in Middlesboro recently wrote to the firm saying he had a Graphophone purchased 15 years before and it was as good as ever except for being out of date. That the music it reproduces is satisfactory even to a trained and critical musician and composer, is demon- strated by the pleasure his Graphophone affords Mr. Hutchinson. Why not have one in your home? Write for "Price Book 20" to Columbia Phonograph Company, General, 64 and 66 Oxford Street, London,W.

div.head: Examinee, Saturday September 14, 1907.
div.p: The Examinee, Saturday September 14, 1907.

decided to start a Golf Club up there. It was a small nine hole course, but we did not despise the day of small beginnings. Now there are several links in the Engadine including a really fine course at Samaden which ranks in the very forefront of Contin- ental links. (Hear, hear.) And if the progress which golf has already made in the Engadine is quite remarkable, I am very certain that as time goes on more and more golfers will be tempted to take their summer holidays in that beautiful valley where the scenery, climate, fine turf and first rate golf are all of them such attractions. (Hear, hear). And now the game is taking root in other parts of Switzerland, and so, what a few years since was our infant Association, has grown into a fine healthy bairn, which has every prospect of a flourishing and suc- cessful career in the future. (Hear, hear). Each season new clubs are affiliated to our Association, and its influence is likely to spread even beyond the borders of Switzerland. I have not yet seen the club started at Montana, but from all accounts alike in point of turf, style of the links and the beauty of the surroundings this splendid course is, or very soon will be, second to no other golf links anywhere on the Continent, and it is a great feather in the cap of Colonel Jameson, and my friend, Mr. Hay Gordon, who have taken such an interest in it. (Hear, hear.) Now Geneva is making preparations for a good 18 hole course, and that in the neighbourhood of such a centre of population will be an important addition to golf in Switzerland. (Hear, hear.) We have in Lucerne here a thoroughly sporting, interesting and picturesque nine hole muse at the Sonnenberg, which is capital fun—(hear, hear) —and I certainly hope it won't be very long before in this very central position of Switzerland there is a good 18 hole course. (Hear, hear.) So, on the whole, I think we have good reason to congratulate ourselves, and the progress of golf in Switzerland is sure to be stimu- lated and strengthened now we have associated with 'it our friend Colonel Woodward, (Cheers) who has such wide experience, and who has done so much for the game on the Riviera and more recently in the Engadine. (Cheers.) Ladies and gentlemen, before I sit down I have a very pleasant duty to perform in asking Mr. Morgan whom one always listens to with mingled feelings of envy and enjoyment, to propose what is at once the most delightful and most important toast of the even ing the health of the ladies. ( ipplause.) Mr. Morgan said :—" Mr. President, Ladies and Gentleman, I have no doubt you will find my reputa- tion as a speaker is founded on the story I related some little time since at one of our golf meetings about Daniel in the lion's den when he remarked, "Thank Heaven, there'll be no after-dinner speeches at this banquet! " Mach laughter.) I believe I was elected Captain of the Lucerne Golf Club because I don't know anything at all about the game; and I suppose I am now asked to propose the health of the ladies for the same reason, because I cannot say I know anything about them. (Cries of "Oh " and laughter.) Well, if , I did I certainly would not tell what I think of them while my wife is listening. (Renewed laughter). Baron Pfyffer said "I do not know why our President was so kind as to ask me to say a word. I may men- ticn that I was the only Swiss who took an interest in golf here in Lucerne when the game was first started; and so I could tell you lots of the early history of golf here. But our host has already been so kind as to mention Mr. Morgan and Mr. Mansfield who have helped us so mach, and I join him in heartily thanking these gentleman for the assistance they have given to golf in Lucerne. Our host has said that he hoped it would not be very long before we had an 18-hole course here. As far as I can help that object I shall do so. (Loud cheers). I ask you to drink to the success of the Swiss Golf Association. (Renewed cheers).

div.head: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. Trade Unionists and Insurance.
div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. Trade Unionists and Insurance.
The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in Beld-street schools on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Plumb presiding. INSURANCE AGENTS' GRIEVANCE.

Mr. AIoonFIELD introduced the question of the attitude of trade unionists towards lfTe assurance agents. He stated that at a meeting of the Warrington branch of the National Union of Life Assurance Agents a resolution was passed viewing with great dissatis- faction the very unsatisfactory attitude adopted by the trade unionists affiliated with the Trades and Labour Council towards the Union agents. Although nearly twelve months had elapsed since they had issued 4,000 circulars as an earnest appeal and also advertised in the annual report, the results were almost nil as regarded the practical support which they expected after the unanimous endorsement of the appeal by the TratiAß COMICiI. They .;ucerely tritht,oa Llxe would rise to a sense of its duty and press for a more effective issue. In the course of a speech on the subject, Mr. Moorfield said the trade unionists had not responded to the appeal to encourage Union agents by giving them their new cases. They had not even asked agents to show their cards of membership and had been indifferent whether they had a union agent to collect from them or not. By acting in that way they were encouraging agents outside the Union to defiantly say: "What is the use of joining your Union when we can obtain the support of trade unionists without doing so ?" The Union was the only one that had for its object the uplifting of men to one standard rate of commission and interest and defended its members In Courts of Law. There were about twelve companies who were paying far below the standard rate. The CHAIRMAN said the Union agents had reason to complain, as they were justified in asking for the sup- port of their fellow trade unionists. It was, however, one thing for the Trades Council to say it would do its best and another to compel the members of the branches to do so.

Mr. LEACH pointed out that the appeal to trade unionists was not that they should only support certain offices but that they should give their business to union agents. The union had within its ranks representatives of all offices.

Tne SECRETARY (Mr. E. Plinston) strongly supported the appeal. He said the vast majority of assurance agents were working at a smaller rate of commission than the friendly sooiety then and the menace was that the commission of the friendly societies would be brought down to the rate of the companies. Mr. Smrni said the majority of the trade unionists belonged to friendly societies. Mr. PODMORE complained that a great many trade unionists only applied their principles to their own particular societies, and it was difficult to make them realise the importance of a question like this. The Council decided ao endorse the appeal, and call upon affiliated societies to do their utmost to carry it into effect.

div.p: THE NEW RULES.

The SECRSTA.RY said that with regard to this matter, he was sorry he could not report great progress, as only eleven out of twenty-five societies had replied. It was decided to hold a special meeting a fortnight hence, with a view to the new rules becoming operative in October.

div.head: WHITE CITY, fdIINCHESTER.
div.p: WHITE CITY, fdIINCHESTER.
THE LATE REV. E. J. WILLGOCKS.
MEMORIAL TO BE RAISED.
What Form Should It Take?

It was an eloquent testimony to the affection in which the late Rev. E. J. Willocks was held by all associated with him in the work of the Grammar School, that the Council Chamber at the Town Hall was filled with a very repre3entative gathering on Thursday evening when a meeting of Governors, masters, past and present boys was held to consider a suggested memorial to the late headmaster. Mr. C. S. Burgess presided and amongst others present were: —The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), the Revs. Canon Willis, J. S. Forbes,and F. H. Cooke (Sedgfield, Durham), Messrs. Carruthers, Young, Herzog, and Rossiter (members of the Grammar School staff ),Alder- man Bennett, Councillor Wilding, Messrs. A. Browne, C. D. Parkinson, H. Collin,R. Dobson, W. E. Atkin, S. Wallhead and J. H. Smethurst (secretary of the Old Boys' Union).

The SECRETARY announced the receipt of letters of apology for non-attendance from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Mr. Vera B. Davies, Revs. Canon Gibson Smith, T. A. Schonberg (Withington), E. A. Hutchinson (Wiggington), and J. A. Hannah (Training College, Norwich), Messrs. Henry Roberts, W. Milne Leather, H. Adams, W. R. Hannah (Preston), Arthur Down, F. C. Scotson (Manchester), W. Bain- bridge (Walton), H. Gorse (Liverpool), D. G. Dale (Leigh), J. Bamforth, and H. W. Longdin (Penge, London). Mr.Gorse,of Liverpool,wrote : Whatever else is done, I think a memorial tablet should be put in the Parish Church which is bound up with the Boteler Grammar School in the memories of all old boys, but I do not think that would be enough. A marbie bust is probably out of the question ; a scholarship, prizes founded in his memory—all these occur to one, but whatever is done I know it will be well done for the honour of the old Boteler Grammar School and for the love we all bore him. I hope time will be given to enable old boys scattered over all parts of the world to send their mite. Only the other day I ran across an old boy at Newcastle-on-Tyne who had not heard of his death and was much cut up about it. He had been talking about him the night before. The CHAIRMAN said they were invite], there by the Committee of the Old Boys' Union, through the courtesy of the Mayor' to consider the raising of a memorial to their old friend and master the Rev. E. J. Willcocks who, as they knew, for a very long period first as an assistant and later as headmaster, was con- nected with the Grammar School. Their presence was, he took it, an evidence ef their affection for their old master, their sympathy with Mrs. Willcocks and her family, and the interest they took in the old school. The Committee of the Old Boys' Union had held 3 meeting, and passed a resolution that it was desirable to raise a memorial to Mr. Willcocks, and also decided to call a meeting of governors, masters, and past and present boys to act in conjunction with the committee of the Old Boys' Union, to collect subscriptions and otherwise further the founding of the memorial.

div.head: VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.
div.p: VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.

Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE moved a vote of condolence with Mrs. Willcocks and family. He thought that was a most fitting occasion on which to pass such a resolu- tion, as it was the first meeting of old Batelerians there had been since the death of the late esteemed headmaster. Mr. COLLIN seconded.

The CHlmmiN,--irTsupporting, said he had known Mr. Willcocks longer than any man now living in War- rington and no-one had a greater regard for him. He was a boy in the sixth form 371 years ago when Mr. Willcocks came to the Grammar School as second master and the friendship between them continued up to the time of Mr. Willcocks' death. He (Mr. Burgessl felt more than he could say on that occasion. The resolution was carried in silence, all standing. COMMITTEE APPOI NTE D.
The following resolutions ware put from the chair and passed seriatim

(1)- That a committee be elected to act in conjunc- tion with the Committee of the Old Boys, Union for raising a memorial to the late Rev. E. Willcocks, M.A. (2) That such Committee now to be elected shall consist of one representative of the governors, three representatives of the old boys (not members of the Committee of the Old Boys' Union), and two repre- sentatives of the present boys. (3) That the Joint Comnaittee shall have power t o add to its number and that a quorum shall consist of not less than seven members.

(4) That the Joint Committee shall have power to delegate its duties or any of them to a sub-committee consisting of not less than seven members, of whom five shall form a quorum. Messrs. Arthur Browne, Horace Sankey and H. Collin reprssent the old boys on the committee. The other represen atives will ba a ppointed in due course.
THE MEMORIAL. SUGGESTIONS AS TO ITS FORA.

The CHAIRMAN then expressed his willingness to receive suggestions as to the form the memorial should take, and said the Committee would endeavour to carry out the wishes of the subscribers, as far as possible. It had been suggested—and the proposal appealed to him more strongly than anything else—that they should found a scholarship. That, of course, was no easy matter and would mean the collection of a large sum of money. It had been suggested that if that could not be done,they should found a Prize. That was a very laudable object, but it did not appeal to him as the other proposal did. Other suggestions were that they should put a stained glass window in the Parish Church ; that something should be done in Orford Church ; and that a tablet should be placed in the Parish Church or the school. The Rev. J. S. FORBES, having promised to convey the expression of sympathy, said he felt sure that every- one who subscribed would desire that the memorial should meet with the wishes of his old headmaster. Mr. Willcocks' whole heart and life were in the school. It was perfectly true that he worked at Orford, and had a great affection for the place, and that the people of Orford had a great affection for him. It was true also that he was connected with the Parish Church and loved it, but his whole-hearted affection was .in the school, and he (Mr. Forbes) honestly felt that any memorial should be connected with the place which he loved so intensely.

The Rev. F. H. COOKE suggested that they should build the chancel of the new church at Orford and in that way unite the school and Orford in the ntemorial. He had written to Canon Gibson Smith who replied that he thought the suggestion was admirable. " Xhe fact that his rnemcrial would be so closely connected with that of Mrs. Beamont and with the scene of his early labours." wrote the Canon, " would, I feel sure, have commended itself to him strongly. He always enjoyed recalling his work at Orford where he made his first home. It was always connected in his mind with the memory of his friend Mr. William Sharp, who was deeply interested in the place and is jointly com- memorated in the church."

Mr. C. D. PARKINSON was strongly in favour of the foundation of a scholarship. Alderman BENNETT said that while the primary memorial should be associated with the school, he thought the idea of a tablet at the Parish Church,where Mr. Willcock read the lessons with such power, was an excellent one. Whether a chancel at Orford was feasible or not, it would be possible for the Orford people themselves to mark their appreciation of Mr. Willcocks. He (Alderman Bennett) was particularly impressed with the suggestion to place a bust in the school as it would be an inspiration to all future generations of Grammar School boys. Mr. PARKINSON thought that whatever shape the memorial took, it should be one of utility. Mr. CARRUTHERS said that if they could not raise .Cl5OO to endow a scholarship of £5O a year, they might put aside a certain sum for the development of a good school library. The CWAIR3IAN said that if they could raise £l,OOO and found a scholarship of £3O a year, it would be a worthy memorial and a grand thing to achieve. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Mayor, who said the Town Hall could not be better used than for an object connected with such a noble institution as the Grammar School.

div.head: REV. THOMAS MILLER.
div.p: THE REV. THOMAS MILLER.
HIS IMPRESSIONS OF "BEAUTIFUL

religious activity. He stood a few minutes the other night watching people go into a public-house. He saw women carrying little children there and heard language that was appalling. Within five minates walk of that church he saw women who ought to have been taking care of children at home, taking them after nine o'clock into the public house. He said that if it required the Church to sacrifice what pride it had got, it should be done in order to get the people and raise them to Jesus Christ. They would never enter into the Kingdom of Heaysn by pride. Mr. Miller touched upon the decay of family life and urged a revival of family prayers. He hoped the coming year would be successful, not in the mere numbers or in preaching, but in souls brought to a real knowledge of Christ. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: WARRINGTON."
div.p: WARRINGTON."
Vigorous Speech.

At Bold-street Wesleyan church on Thursday the Rev. Thomas Miller (the newly-appointed minister to the Warrington circuit) received a cordial welcome at the hands of his future colleagues and congregation. In the afternoon Mr. Miller preached an eloquent sermon and in the evening a public meeting was held presided over by Mr. John Upson. Amongst those present were the Revs. Sidney Pitt, W. Mellor, J. Gunnell and E. J. Gawne, Mr. R. H. IVleldrum, Mr. Frank A. Harris, and representatives of all the churches in the circuit. There was a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN in welcoming Mr. Miller said he had already made himself known to a surprising number of the members of the church and congregation and he had met with remarkable success in his pulpit ministra- tions. They not merely welcomed him but they could assure him that he would get their loyal support ii whatever he did. (Hear, hear.) The work in the circuit was making great progress and they were very pleasant duties indeed. The membership had increased so far as the church was concerned. The church had met with a great success but they had still plenty to do. When they had got the church full they would be satisfied. He extended a very hearty welcome to Mr. Miller and he hoped and trusted God would keep him in health and strength so that he could do his work successfully. (Applause.) The Rev. SIDNEY PITT in welcoming Mr. Miller said they had sustained a great loss in losing Mr. Manning. They ought not to expect the new minister at once to do everything that Mr. Manning used to do but later on perhaps he would do all that Mr. Manning did. He hoped Mr. Miller would do his utmost for the welfare of the circuit as a whole, and that the member- ship would keep on increasing as it had done in the past. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. H. MELDRUM also extended to Mr. Miller a hearty welcome. The Rev. W. MELLOR said he hoped the church would increase spiritually, that Mr. Miller would enjoy his change,and that he would have a very successful career. He would have the support of the people and he (Mr. Mellor) hoped the church would hold the same position that it occupied a quarter of a century ago. The class meetings were not attended as they should be, by any means. The annual conference in connection with their Church was going worse every year. Documents were put in and read, but the best place for those documents was the fire. (Laughter.) They were read and that was all. The Holy Communion was not attended as it should be. Some peop!ta never thought of going at all, whilst others went about once every year, and that he much regretted. He hoped that people would take more notice of the Holy Communion, and also of the class meetings. The latter were not progressing. In refer- ring to the attendance at the communion service, he said at one time they used to get 50 or GO, but now they only got about twenty, and sometimes not that. The prayer meetings at Penketh were well attended but in Warrington hardly anybody went. He hoped there would be a great revival of activity throughout tho circuit, and that Mr. Miller's ministry would be blessed with the highest results. (Applause.) The Rev. JOHN GUNNELL assured Mr. Miller that there was plenty of scope for useful work in the circuit. It was a pleasant sphere of labour and he would find no friction. If he (Mr. Gunnell) were beginning his ministerial life over again he would not wish for happier associations,as far as colleagues were concerned, than Mr. Miller would have. He would find that the officers were loyal and devoted to their church, bearing very great affection to their ministers, and doing their utmost to advance the interests of Methodism and the cause of Christ. The societies were also united and as far as his observations went,there was a steady increase in the congregations, with scarcely any exception, throughout the circuit. The people were expecting great things and he (Mr. Gunnell) hoped they were prepared to attempt great things for good. With that spirit of exceptancy influencing their ministers, office bearers and members,they might look confidently to times of great prosperity and ingathering. There was tiome risk in these days lest the multiplicity of social engage- ments should thrust aside what they understood by true evangelical work. He was not by any means sure that the old methods of doing evangelistic work would serve in the coming years. They would perhaps have to be modified, but after all, methods were secondary. There was throughout the circuit a very urgent need of a great revival of religion in the hearts of their own people and of a revival in the larger sense of an in- gathering into the Church of Christ. Might their hopes be reaiized and their prayers answered. (Applause.)
the CHAIRMAN said Mr. William Bennett, the senior steward at Padgate, was unable to be present, but all the churches were represented and united in the welcome to Mr. Miller.

Mr. FRANK A. HARRIS, in welcoming Mr. Miller in the name of Bold-street Church, said they had had a taste of his pulpit powers and they were delighted with him. Another thing which der.idedly attracted him (Mr. ilurio to mt. Miller was the fact that he lost no time in getting to work aud the first Sunday saw him in the Sunday school. Without disparaging any other organisations, he (Mr. Harris) believed that in the Sunday schools was the hope of the future. He know that Mr. Miller was delighted with Warrington and he vwped his residence nmonast them would be happy and fruitful in good work. Mr. Manning was good enough to lead them to great things in that church and they stood by him. As they stood by Mr. Manning so would they stand by Mr. Miller. (Applause.) The Rev. THOMAS MILLER, who had a very hearty reception, said that Warrington was much better than ever he thought. The last time he was in Warrington was when he was returning from Ireland. He had been out on the boat all night and was wet through, and to make things doubly comfortable, it was raining, so that his impressions at that time were .that Warrington was not a place where the railway companies need state on their tourist guides that passengers might break their journey. (Laughter.) He confessed that opinion had changed and he had already ventured to say to one who went to Ireland very often that he might break the journey at Warring- ton, and he would find that there were a lot worse places, and that not a great many industrial towns were equal to it in beauty. (Applause.) He had read the words Beautiful Warrington—he believed on an " Examiner " placard—a score of times since he came to Warrington. They fascinated one,because one did not generally find associated with Lancashire towns the idea of much.imauty. The surroundings at Bold-street were beautiful. No one could wish fora finer situation for a house; no one could have a finer building to preach in ; and there could be no finer church premises in any town. Through the buildings and the member- ship of that Church there should be a Beautiful War- rington, not only in the shape of trees and open spaces but that the men and women whose chmacters might not be very beautiful might be transformed by the grace of God. After all, it was the moral character and spiritual condition of the people which decided whether a place was beautiful or not. Everyone who sought to train a mind, brighten a home, change a life, and improve the surroundings, whether he was a Methodist or not, whether he was a religious man or not, had his (Mr. Miller's) greatest sympathy and approval. Mr. Miller thr paid a high tribute to the work of Mr. Manning s reflected in the sound financial position of the Char h and the influence for good which he had exercised on the lives of the people. Continuing, he spoke on the spiritual needs of to-day. They were living, he said, in times of great commercial prosperity and expansion. It could be said that the English people had never been so prosperous as they were at the present time, as far as material things were concerned. But it did not always follow that spiritual intensity increased with raaterial prosperity. There was one prayer of St. Paul's that always came to his mind when he saw people getting on in a worldly sense and dying down in spiritual things: " May thou prosper as thy soul prospers." He hoped everybody would be made a pauper if with increasing wealth there was the lessening of spiritual fervour. There was with commercial prosperity a danger lest the spiritual life, which was infinitely more important than business success, should be neglected and they should settle down into a state of respectability which was far away from true religious fervour. Outwardly,from the moral standpoint England had made rapid strides, but if they took teats they were sometimes tempted to get discouraged. The danger was that they should rest contented with their worldly prosperity. They had a magnificent church—hut why? Not that someone should get into the church and feel very comfort- able and be interested for a few hours by the music,reading and sermon, but that through that church the neighbourhood should know the power of Jesus. Church music could not be too good but the purpose of a fine organ and musical service should not be financial profit and entertainment, but to drive home the message of love to the hearts of the people. If they gained everything else and lost that, they were a complete failure as a church. He did not believe in a church that was a mere preaching place, but he believed in preaching. There was no honour so great as that of being a preacher of the Gospel and no work commanded greater study than preparation for the pulpit. Some people were always afraid of playing to the gallery but it only meant that the preacher touched the common nature and the common heart. He would rather have someone in the gallery to play to than that there should be nobody there. The pew rent system was a grand system if it was interpreted rightly and he had not the I slightest desire to have free seats. There should, how- ever, be an understanding on the part of seat-holders that three minutes before the service began the seats should be thrown open to the public. They had no right to reserve a seat to shut out a person,not even to gain a pew rent, and if the system were used in that way it would become, a curse. They did not need to turn their 'old chapels into the element of the mission ball that was the music hall. Those halls were doing a grand work in 1 their place, but since the chapel could not do that, let I the people feel that that was a circuit chapel and through the circuit life they might make it a centre of 1

div.head: GOLF AT LUCERNE.
div.p: GOLF AT LUCERNE.
Mk A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., BEATS ,BOGIE
And Gives a Dinner and a Dance.

We have just received news of Mr. A. H. Crosfield's doings in Switzerland, where he is the popular President of the Swiss Golf Association and one of the founders of the name in that country. By Mr. Crosfield's request the Secretary of the Lucerne Golf klub sends us the following account of recent events IL golf circles at lovely Lucerne. The Lucerne golf week has come and gone and left in its wake memories the most satisfactory, and has added another record to the annals of this sporting 1 and hospitable club. The weather on Monday was I not too kind in the afternoon and all Tuesday the elements rained thoughtlessly. Later it cleared and on Wednesday and Thurszlay conditions were the most favourable. At the prize presentation on this latter day there were many present at the "at home" when Mrs. Gaw handed to the winners the various trophies they had won. This lady was introduced by Mr. Robert Mansfield the Captain, and later Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., the President of the Swiss Golf Association, thanked Mrs. Gaw and said a few words about the Swiss Golf Association and its work in this country, the progress golf had made in Lucerne, and the great attraction to -this place the links were. He was delighted to find them in such excellent order and looked forward to the day not long distant, when he hoped that Lucerne would have its eighteen hole course second to none on the Continent, where the Swiss Championships could be played in turn with such links as Samaden. _ _

On Tuesday evening Mr. Crosfield was the host at the dinner he offered to the Swiss Golf Association, members of the Lucerne Golf Club and their friends. There were some fifty covers laid in the private dining room of the National Grand Hotet which was festooned and illuminated with dozens of electric jets. The floral decorations were artistically carried out in pink and white Japanese dahlias and the valuable prizes and Challenge Cups belonging to the Lucerne Golf Club were distributed about. After dinner Mr.Crosfield was the giver of a delightful dance at which there were some two hundred present. This festival went on well into the small hours of the morning, the while to first rate music and with a floor that is second to none anywhere. At the dinner Mx. Mansfield gave the health of "our host" which was drunk with enthusiasm and "For he's a jolly good fellow." The President of the S.G.A. responded in his usual happy manner. Mr. H. H. Morgan, the former Captain of the Club, gave the toast " The Ladies," and to this Mr. S. March responded. The principal event at the golf meeting was for the Championship of Lucerne, for the Sonneuburg Cup. The Champion of Switzerland for the past two years, Mr. H. L. Gaw, was first favourite and he met in the final the President of the S.G.A. who had vanquished in the semi-finals Mr. J. L. Welch, having made the remarkable amateur record of 33 for the first eight holes. "A. H." was in fine form, his score thus far being two under the "Colonel." Wet weather pre- vented the play proceeding as it was advisable to rest the greens. The final proved fatal to Mr. A. H. Cro 'field, who fell before the ever-conquering Phila- delphian, Mr. Gaw, by 5 and 4., Mr. Crosfield taking the runner-up cup offered by Mr. G. E. van der Hooven.

For the Blumenthal Cup there were ten cards returned with Mr. J. L. Welch at the head with the creditable 77, less 3, equal 74, four under bogey, and next to him was Mr. C. F. Ulrich 97 less 22, equals 75. He won the Baroness Hans Pfyffer's prize. Mr. Gaw received the best gross score cup. Mr. J. L. Welch also took the gold medal which can only go to a permanent member of the Lucerne Golf Club. The Ladies' H.C.P. opened in the afternoon when Miss Cassells secured the siver cream and sugar basin. given by Captain Henry M. Jones, V.C. The Lucerne Gold Medal fell to Mrs. S. H. March as well as the second prize offered by Mr. Louis Stern. The Swiss Golf Association Challenge Cup, which is played for annually at Lucerne, the captain of the club Mr. R obert E. Mansfield secured, doing the first eighteen holes in 90 less 14 equal 70, the second in 92 less 14 equal 78, giving a net lotal of 154,0 r two below bogey ' for the thirty six. The captain also secured the Countess Apraxine's prize a silver hunting knife which she gives annually for this event. Mrs. C. J. Reade for the third time in succession qualified for the ladies Swiss Golf Association Challenge Cup given by the Lucerne Golf Club, and thereby won it outright. She also won the bwnze medal play off., a silver ciaampagne cup. l'he approacni..sl4zaLeu fen w me hon. secretary of the Lake of Como Golf Club, Mr. F. N. Blundell after tying with Mr. Maw at 9. The ladies approaching was very exciting as Miss Chambers the hon. secretary of the North Warwickshire Golf Club, tied with Mrs. March and a close contest fol- lowed which Miss Chambers won. The men's prize was given by Mrs. S. H. March, and the ladies by Mr. Louis Sterne, the former a silver antique wine taster, the latter a silver scent bottle. At the putting competition on Thursday for the Captain and Mrs. Mansfield's prizes, and a second ladies prize given by Mrs. C. J. Reade, Mr. Crosfield, Mr. H. L. Gaw and Mr. H. S. Ashington all tied at 15. In the play off the Champion fell off and the President of the S.G.A. (Mr. Crosfield) did a clean 14, winning. There was also a tie between Miss Chambers, Mrs. Jameson and Miss Darlington the hon. secretary of the Ladies' ' Midland Golf Association and Captain of the Ladies' Warwickshire County Golf Club. Miss Darlington won by doing a superb and faultless 12 all square with bogey. This presentation of the prizes brought to termination a very pleasant afternoon and conclu- sion of a capital golfing tournament.

Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission. Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the above place of worship on Sunday. Mr. J. Upson was the preacher in the morning, and at the evening service Mr. G. Davey-Smith occupied the pulpit. In the after- noon the service was conducted by the Rev. Thomas Miller (newly-appointed minister). There were good congregations throughout the day, and at each service anthems and special hymns were rendered by the choir. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held, when the fruit, vegetables, &c., with which the interior of the building had been tastefully decorated, were disposed of. Songs were rendered by Misses Haviour and Horton and Messrs. Bennett and Perrin, and during the evening refreshments were handed round. Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Church.

At this church on Sunday the -Rev. Thomas Miller, the newly-appointed minister to the Warrington circuit, preached the anniversary sermons to large congrega- tions. In the afternoon a service of song was held entitled "Pilgrims' Progress." The connective read- ings were given by Mrs. Johnson (Penketh). Mr. A. Horrocks presided. Mr. E. G. Rickers and Mr. C. Muir discharged the duties of organist and choirmaster respectively. The morning subject was "Zeal and caution," The preacher said the greatest risks were justifiable in the service of Christ, but there must also be discretion.—ln the evening Mr. Miller took for his test: "And the very God of Peace sanctify you wholly ; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is He that calleth you, Who also will do it." The subject of his discourse was Perfection of Christian life." The opposition to the missionaries in Christian service was dealt with.
Christian Missions in China.
The Rev. John Yonge on Dr. Morrlson's Work.

The Rev. John Yonge preached at Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-street, on Sunday, the subject being "Robert Morrison, D.D., Pioneer of Protestant Christian missions in China, who landed in Canton 100 years ago, September Bth, 1807." The text was: " Behold I have set before thee an open door" Rev. lii. S. He said that in the history of the Christian Church, the BthSep- tember,lBo7 was a red letter day.On this day one hundred years ago, there set foot on the soil of China the first Protestant Christian Missionary. It must be stated, however, to the lasting honour of the church of Rome that even centuries earlier, in the person of the heroic Francis Xavier,she bad effected an entrance in that fastly shut empire of the East. For many long years Xavier patiently and resolutely waited at the door persisting in importunate prayer,crying with ceaseless& persistence "Rock ! Rock! when wilt thou open ? " At length he found admission for himself and his faith and his church. The Protestant and Evangelical Faith had neither sought nor found entrance in China until that day one hundred years ago, when Robert Morrison entered the city of Canton. Now it was the story of that remarkable and devoted life, and what had followed upon it which he told them that evening. He called attention to it not Only because of its intrinsic interest in the history of Christian missions, but because of the splendid illustration it afforded of an entirely conse- crated life, and because of the example it offered to the young Christian manhood of this thetwentietla century. The Preacher then briefly sketched the career of Dr. Morrison, and referring to the persevance which char- acterised his early life, he said, that in nearly every case in which a great life had evolved from humble and obscure beginnings it had been the product of strenuous and persistent self-denial, of unstinting and unwearying effort; of abstinence from those recreations and pastimes which so many youths pursued in these days with such supreme and laborious devotion. Only toe frequently we found,young men especially,who pro- fessed to be thelplea of Chrilt becoming so weary with the work and the recreations of the week that they devoted the mornings of the Sabbath to extra indulgence in rest, and seemed to have but scant energy left for any usefulness in the afternoon. Such a use of leisure hours either on week days or Sabbath never yet pro- cured devoted servants of the Cross and never would. Alluding to the attitude of multitudes of so-called Christian people in these days concerning the work of foreign missions, he said he had known and still knew men of considerable intelligence and considerable pro- fession.of belief in the Lord Jesus Christ, who with 'every accent of incredulity and even contempt would repudiate foreign missions as even absurd and futile. They would argue that the religion of a country which had come down from past ages,was good enough for the people to whom it had come, and that especially the hoary and venerable religions of the East were too engrained in the Eastern mind and nature to be ever uprooted and overthrown. They forgot that if it had not been for the Christian Missionaries in the early history of our own islands, they might have been in the dense darkness of moral and spiritual night to this day, and they were blind also to the facts of this last century during which the Gospel of Christ had reclaimed whole races of savages from barbarism and had even permeated the lands of the East with moral light and liberty. The facts were against the scaptics. Dr.Nlorrison's work was slow, indeed, in coming to fruition. At the close of his marvellous career he could only count ten converts as the numerical result of all his 27 years of work. The vast and even mighty linguistic achievements which he did accomplish, made the future prosecution of Christian Missions much more possible for his successors. As soon as he mastered the language so that he might teach and preach in it, he set himself to translate the scriptures. In six years he completed the New Testament and in twelve years he produced the first volume of his Anglo-Chinese dictionary and within 13 years he finished it, in six large quarto volumes. Mr. Yonge then alluded to the facts about the Gospel in China to-day There were now more than 15,000 church members who represented a Christian community of half a million people. They were to be found scattered, throughout the Empire, and were as lights shining in dark places. Throughout China now there were more than 3,000 foreign missionaries, including wives, and many of the latter were among the very best of missionaries. These European and American missionaries were aided by about 10,000 picked and qualified native agents, who worked as pastors, evangelists, colporteurs, hospital assistants, and teachers of schools. There were now in China thousands of chapels, many of which the converts themselves had built and paid for. There were hundreds of hospitals and dispensaries, homes for lepers, asylums for the blind and the insane, 200 boarding schools and colleges for male students, and 93 for females, wherein 290 male and 270 female teachers were at work. There were more than 1,350 day schools and upwards of 10,000 male and 7,000 female scholars. The centenary of Morrison and of the evangelical missions in China, con- cluded the preacher, was a new call to all of them to cherish missionary enthusiasm.

• EIFFEL'S TOILET. For the third time since its erection in 1809, the. Eiffel Tower is performing its toilet. It is as well that the process is not more frequent, seeing that it costs £3,000. For the first three renewals the colour was orange, but last time they changed it to gold. Now it is td 'be silver white from the third platform upward, iron and brown lower down. Forty men will be at work for three months, and 300 pintals of paint will be used.

Warrington Man Killed in London. At the Hammersmith Coroner's Court, on Saturday, Mr. Ingleby Oddie held an inquest on the body of Joshua Thornton, thirty-five, a boilermaker, of Greenall-street, Warrington, who died in the West London Hospital. The deceased was engaged by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company,of War- ringtr,n,on contract work at the Hammersmith Distillery erecting some large iron tanks,and on Thursdak,whilst engaged movirg a large iron side (weighing nearly a tin and a quarter) through a doorway by means of a block and a pulley attached to a cross beam, the latter collapsed, and the deceased was struck by the falling iron and fatally injured. Fellow-workmen were not sure whether the beam slipped from its supports owing to the swing or whether the beam gave way. It was stated that. the deceased was a healthy man and an ex-member of the Warrington F.C. team. The jury considered that the foreman should have' exercised a little more discretion, and returned a 1 verdict of "Accidental death."
